Dolly Parton – a life in pictures

Beloved musician, actor and philanthropist Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80 after an incredible, one-of-a-kind career. The star was known for both her fierce wit and her unflappable positivity.

In a life filled with much-quoted gems of wisdom, here are some of her finest:

“The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain.”

“You have to work at being happy. Some people work at being miserable. If I wake up in the morning and don’t feel great or things are not great, I try to think about what I can do to make things work better, rather than just falling into that deep hole, because then you just go deeper and deeper.”

“If you see someone without a smile today, give ’em yours.”

“If you’re feeling low, don’t despair. The sun has a sinking spell every night, but it comes back up every morning.”

“They think I’m simple-minded because I seem to be happy. Why shouldn’t I be happy? I have everything I ever wanted and more. Maybe I am simple-minded. Maybe that’s the key: simple.”

“Happiness is your commitment to appreciating all that is good in life.”

“A positive attitude and a sense of humor go together like biscuits and gravy.”

“I’m not going to limit myself just because people won’t accept the fact that I can do something else.”

“I always say I’ve dreamed myself into a corner. I’ve got to keep all those dreams alive. Every dream spins off into some something else.”

“Don’t get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life.”

“You’ll never do a whole lot unless you’re brave enough to try.”

“I hope to die right in the middle of a song and right on the stage doing what I love to do. I hope to be about 120 when that happens.”

“My music is so mine, it’s hard to turn it over to someone else. I have to be really involved in the production. It’s like someone else taking care of your kids – if they don’t treat them well, you’re going to be pissed off.”

“I never tried quitting, and I never quit trying.”

“Above everything else I’ve done, I’ve always said I’ve had more guts than I’ve got talent.”

“I think in a way, my music has been almost like my ministry. Hopefully, it’s healing in some ways, just having a good sense of humor to be able to lift people up, to have songs that people can relate to.”

“It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”

“People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don’t know, I’m never there.”

“I’m not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb – and I’m not blonde either.”

“I have pretty good skin considering my age, and I think a lot of it is mineral oil and bacon grease.”

“I describe my look as a blend of Mother Goose, Cinderella and the local hooker!”

“I’m not like a real person. I love being artificial. I think there’s a little magic in the fact that I’m so totally real, but look so artificial at the same time.”

“I am a self-made woman, and I have the doctor bills to prove it.”

“I’m no natural beauty. If I’m gonna have any looks at all, I’m gonna have to create them.”

“A lot of people have said I’d have probably done better in my career if I hadn’t looked so cheap and gaudy. But I dress to be comfortable for me, and you shouldn’t be blamed because you want to look pretty.”

“Those people who wake up and they’re just beautiful, they’re just born that way. Well, that ain’t me. I gotta work for everything I’ve got.”

“I always love working with children. I never had children of my own. God has his purposes. God didn’t let me have children so everybody’s children could be mine. That’s kind of how I’m looking at it.”

“Love is something sent from heaven above to worry the hell out of you.”

“I was blessed to have family members who encouraged me to pursue my dreams. Whether it is your parents, or your uncles or your aunts or even the neighbor down the road, it’s important that kids have someone who encourages them to chase their rainbow.”

“I often get myself in love trouble because I’m so passionate; I love so much and so deep.”

“Love is like a butterfly: as soft and gentle as a feather, many-colored and full of cheer.”

“I think everyone should be with who they love. I don’t want to be controversial or stir up a bunch of trouble but people are going to love who they are going to love. I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.”

Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 20:00:23 GMT

Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election

Why do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?

Andy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission.

Burnham, a longtime advocate of electoral reform, will be asked to support the new commission into ditching first past the post in his first 100 days as prime minister.

MPs have said the commission must report before the next election and hope to put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission.

New polling of MPs by YouGov suggests the change is now supported by a majority in the Commons. Of those polled, 53% of MPs said they supported a review into first past the post – the current system of voting.

An amendment to launch the commission has been backed by 185 MPs, including a number of former ministers and supporters of the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer.

The amendment has been tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages on 2 September. A Labour source said: “The representation of the people bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference, and that’s what the government is prioritising.

“Andy remains strongly committed to electoral reform, and has indicated this is a matter for a future party manifesto, given a mandate would need to be secured for it.”

Burnham endorsed the call for a national commission on electoral reform at last year’s Labour conference, saying then as mayor of Greater Manchester that he backed “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament.”

The 98 Labour signatories to the amendment, tabled by Labour’s Alex Sobel include influential backbenchers such as Luke Akehurst and Chris Curtis, leading Labour centrists. Overall, MPs have signed from eight parties, as well as independents.

Signatories also include MPs who have recently become ministers and ministerial aides – including the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, communities minister Florence Eshalomi and the prime minister’s parliamentary private secretary and close ally Jo Platt.

However, the newly appointed frontbench MPs may by convention withdraw support for backbench amendments once parliament returns.

A new commission would not require legislation – meaning the amendment itself may end up out of scope of the bill. But MPs intend to use the amendment as a way of signalling to the prime minister the breadth of support for swifter reform.

A national commission could consider a range of other proportional voting systems to replace first past the post, the current system for a general election in the UK which means the winners of the most votes in each constituency are elected. Other systems are used across the UK, including the Scottish parliament, the Welsh parliament and mayoral votes.

In Scottish and Welsh elections, there are votes for a candidate and for a party, so additional members can be elected from a list alongside constituency representatives. In the recent Greater Manchester mayoralty, voters were given a first and second choice.

Sobel said it was time for the prime minister to endorse the push – signed by more MPs than any other amendment in parliament. “Now we know a majority of MPs back this proposal, including a majority of Labour MPs. I know the prime minister is committed to reforming our electoral system and I and all the MPs who signed this amendment want to work with him to set the UK on a road towards fair, modern general elections,” he said.

MPs told the Guardian that Burnham should announce the commission before the October budget. Rachel Blake, the former Treasury minister, said: “The PLP agrees with Andy Burnham that first past the post is broken, and that a national commission is the way to get a grip on it. The government should press ahead and launch this process within the prime minister’s first hundred days.”

Akehurst, a member of Labour’s governing national executive committee, said: “Parliament is catching up with the public, most of whom already support electoral reform. Andy Burnham has a good track record on proportional representation, and it’s now hugely popular across the Labour party. He should seize this opportunity.”

Labour MP Lizzi Collinge said first past the post “particularly devalues the votes of renters, young people and BAME people, and delivers parliaments that do not represent what most people voted for.”

Another former Labour minister, Catherine Fookes, said first past the post “can’t cope with modern, multiparty politics. Andy Burnham has long talked about the need to move to a fair, proportional system. If he acts now by setting up a commission, he will find that most MPs support him from across parliament – and make good on his promise to rewire British politics.”

A sixth Labour MP, Mike Reader, said that the poll of MPs showed there had been “a sea change in support for PR across Labour and the public. Most MPs know it is the fair thing for the country, it’s just a matter of how we get there. We hope Andy Burnham will now stick to his guns.”

Labour members at the party’s annual conference in 2022 had previously backed a move towards proportional representation, which Burnham called a “historic vote” and said would be a move towards “a country that works for everybody, where everyone’s vote counts”.

Campaign groups said they hoped Burnham would seize the moment for reform while he had a workable parliamentary majority. Make Votes Matter chief executive Emma Harrison said: “I’ve spoken alongside Andy in favour of proportional representation, I know he supports it – now he must show the public he deserves our trust.”

The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum was held to ask whether to change to an alternative vote system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference.

Root reads from same old script in latest episode of England’s off-field soap opera

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 19:00:22 GMT

Captain followed trend of discussing nightclub incidents rather than cricket before the second Test against Pakistan

England won the first game of their last Test series, against New Zealand at Lord’s, but between that match and the second Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were involved in a headline-grabbing incident at a London nightclub. “I’m angry, frustrated at having to sit here and talk through this,” Rob Key said a couple of days later.

“I feel disappointed that I’m here talking about this because there’s so much we’ve tried to do, so much we’ve tried to learn from, and I believe that as a team, the way they’ve carried themselves in the lead‑up to last week’s game, the way they played that Test match – to then be now talking about this, is just incredibly frustrating.”

England won the first game of this Test series, against Pakistan at Headingley, but between that match and the second Brydon Carse was involved in a headline‑grabbing incident at a Derby nightclub. “If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off. I’m really disappointed that after last week’s performance we’re sat here talking about something not related to it at all,” Joe Root said a couple of days later.

“I look at all of the great things we did in that game – I thought the bowlers were outstanding, with the bat there were a couple of times we found ourselves under pressure and we worked our way through it. Every time we sit here and we’re talking about something off the field it’s really frustrating.”

Two months and four days separated the two press conferences, a period in which a great deal changed for this team – the New Zealand series was lost, as was a coach and a captain – but also, it seems, nothing at all. So the frustration expressed by both Key and Root is also being felt, for different reasons, by those who have had to listen to them. Graham Gooch once famously asked Ian Botham, as it happens after a Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, where the teams will be reunited on Thursday: “Who writes your scripts?” Whoever is scripting the latest series of the soap opera needs to do a bit less recycling and get some fresh ideas.

Root suggests that this is now guaranteed, given that since the squad reassembled in London he has led them through “conversations about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England … a very robust discussion about where we currently sit”. The players now know the standards of behaviour expected from them on and off the field. “I think there’s real clarity there, and now the guys can concentrate on focusing on what is important this week, and making sure we prepare properly and diligently for all the challenges that this surface and Pakistan are going to provide.”

It is not just bewildering but damning that after Harry Brook’s run‑in with a bouncer in Wellington, after the first Ashes Test was followed by a squad‑break‑cum-stag-do in the Queensland beach resort of Noosa, after the then Test head coach Brendon McCullum promised to “use a firm grip to ensure that we are not making those same mistakes again”, and after Stokes’s and Atkinson’s night at Chelsea’s Rex Rooms, this was a job that still needed doing.

Key, managing director of the England men’s side, was all smiles in the Lord’s sunshine as he watched the team train on Tuesday, apparently not feeling the sense of profound personal humiliation that the need for Root to lead a “robust discussion” might reasonably have provoked. “I don’t think it has to be rocket science,” Root said of a task that a succession of people older and more experienced than him have evidently bungled, if they attempted it at all. “It’s being clear what your responsibilities are as a player and then delivering on that time and time again.”

More than 15 years after his Test debut, and with Stephen Fleming about to become the eighth interim or permanent coach under whom he has played, Root has certainly been through periods when the team had that clarity. But he would not be drawn on when, and under whom, it had been lost. “I don’t want to get caught up in digging up what’s happened before. My concern is what happens moving from this point,” he said.

Burnham mulls insolvency law shake-up to help bring utilities under public control

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 18:13:56 GMT

Exclusive: Rules on special administration seen as potential ‘roadblock’ to reshaping how UK’s essential services are run

Andy Burnham is considering ripping up the country’s insolvency laws to make it easier to bring key utilities such as Thames Water under public control.

Sources have told the Guardian the prime minister is considering a range of options as he seeks ways of delivering on his promise to radically reshape the way England’s water and Britain’s energy companies are run.

One possibility, according to those briefed on his thinking, is to change the so-called special administration regime (SAR) to make it easier to put companies such as Thames Water into insolvency proceedings, and then take control of them afterwards.

The move could pave the way for what Burnham has promised will be a 10-year project to take public control of utilities, but could trigger a legal challenge from creditors to Thames Water, who have promised to fight any attempt to change insolvency laws.

One person briefed on the plans said: “Andy is completely committed to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option for how to achieve that. The special administration regime is one potential roadblock and his team is examining how they might have to change it to deliver on their promises.”

A government source said: “Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. That’s why this government is looking at how we can give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible.”

Burnham promised in his first speech as prime minister to “build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again”.

In June, he told the Guardian he favoured public ownership for Thames Water, which is struggling with a £20bn debt. Emma Reynolds, the former environment secretary, said earlier this year she was opposed to a planned £10bn bailout by existing creditors because it did not offer value for money.

Burnham was expected to make a speech on the water industry in his first few weeks in power, but was briefed by Downing Street officials on how expensive and legally fraught it could be to take public control of companies such as Thames Water.

Ministers denied reports on Tuesday that Burnham had shelved plans to take Thames into administration, but officials said that they were now taking their time to look at every possible route for doing so – including legislative change.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said on Tuesday: “We are taking no options off the table when it comes to Thames Water … The water industry has been failing people for too long. We’ve seen rising bills while the number of serious pollution incidents are off the scale. We’ve got to do more.”

While Burnham has been clear on his desire to take Thames into public ownership, officials say there are two big problems with the special administration regime as it stands.

The first is that companies can only be taken into administration if they are insolvent or unable to provide a basic level of service. Owing to continued support from a group of creditors hoping to take ownership of the company, neither of these are the case.

The second is that once a company enters administration, the administrator is under a legal duty to maximise returns to the creditors, meaning that it will be difficult for the government to take ownership without paying a significant price.

The process is likely to be legally difficult because many of the creditors are US-based hedge funds with a history of taking an aggressive legal approach to protecting their investments.

One possible solution is to use the upcoming water bill to change the terms of the special administration regime altogether.

The plan has been put together by a group of Labour backbenchers, including the former environment committee members Helena Dollimore and Andrew Pakes, alongside the Good Growth Foundation thinktank.

They are suggesting amending the water bill to introduce new triggers for special administration, including lower financial ones and new environmental metrics.

They have also suggested a “bail in” mechanism, similar to that imposed on the banks after the financial crisis. This would force shareholders and creditors to be fully exposed to losses first, thus protecting taxpayers, and give ministers the power to impose losses on shareholders and haircuts on creditors. The process would also be run by regulators rather than the courts, to speed it up.

Praful Nargund, the director of the Good Growth Foundation, said: “By putting emergency legislation in place now we can avoid litigation and ensure the special administration regime protects taxpayers, employees and customers from paying the price for shareholder failure.”

Pakes said: “The challenge is stopping Thames driving the cost of a SAR up through legal challenges and making sure the costs are fairly represented. The difficulty of the SAR process highlights the failure of regulation to create the incentive for water companies to act faithfully.”

However, this approach could still bring legal challenges, with the Thames creditors promising to bring a judicial review against any attempt to change the way the special administration process works.

A source close to the creditors said: “Rejecting a fully funded £10bn turnaround plan and using legislation to force Thames Water into special administration and a new unfinanceable ownership model would be unprecedented and have an extremely negative read across to other struggling water companies.

“It will only result in litigation and the transfer of huge costs and risk to customers and taxpayers, while irretrievably damaging investor confidence in UK-regulated sectors,” said the source.

Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 18:07:47 GMT

Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists

Dolly Parton, US country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80

Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updates

Dolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - video

Share your tributes and memories of Dolly Parton

In December 1977, Dolly Parton submitted to an interview with ABC Television’s Barbara Walters, much against her friends’ advice. Walters was not noted for her deep love and understanding of country music. She was a notoriously tough cookie, a Boston-born, Sarah Lawrence-educated journalist who had battled scarcely believable sexism to become the first female co-host of an American news programme. The month before she met Parton, she had interviewed Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin while they were working out the terms of the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

It was all a very long way from Parton’s world, and the interview has something of the anthropological exercise about it. Walters looks aghast as Parton shows her around her tour bus, her collection of wigs and her “hand-washable and wrinkle-free” stage outfits (“you really like this? To me, it seems like horror”), and sits impassively as Parton sings Coat of Many Colours to her: an impressive feat, given the song’s saga of rural poverty and homespun wisdom is the mother of all tearjerkers from an artist never averse to yanking at her audience’s heartstrings. She asks Parton if people from “where I come from” would call her a hillbilly; regards the singer’s outfit with a jaundiced eye and tells her “you don’t have to look like this”. And, most infamously, she enquires: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?”

“The joke’s on the public,” responds Parton, her smile never slipping. “I know exactly what I’m doing and I can change it any time … I’m sure of myself. I’m sure of my talent.”

It was a TV appearance that told you a lot about public perceptions of Parton in the years when she surged from Nashville fame to international superstardom – an era when you could turn on British TV and find a Canadian duo called MacLean and MacLean performing a mocking song called Dolly Parton’s Tits – and also told you a lot about Parton herself, most notably that, beneath the wig and the rhinestones, she had rather more in common with Walters than anyone might have thought.

Of course she was sure of her talent: by the time she sat down with Walters, she had already written a string of imperishable country standards: not just Coat of Many Colours, but Jolene, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Down from Dover, I Will Always Love You, Little Bird, Kentucky Gambler, Love Is Like a Butterfly, The Bargain Store, The Seeker. Of course she knew exactly what she was doing with her image, based – as she never tired of telling interviewers – on “the town tramp” back in Pittman Center, Tennessee. A woman whose first solo hit was called Dumb Blonde, she used it both to lure in a certain type of country fan (“rednecks with flat tops who bring women who wear short skirts or tight pants,” as one 1970s journalist sniffily put it) and as a kind of glitzy, fluffy shield.

Behind it, she could be subtly subversive. Years before the controversy around Loretta Lynn’s 1975 single The Pill highlighted the issue of Nashville’s sexism, Parton was writing songs of a distinctly feminist bent – Just Because I’m a Woman and When Possession Gets Too Strong among them – even if she always demurred from describing herself as such. She also had a line in songs that could give more conservative Nashville stars palpitations. Down from Dover was extraordinarily beautiful, but it seemed to simmer with empathic rage on behalf of its protagonist, an outcast unmarried mother, and concluded with a description of her giving birth to a stillborn baby. Her duet partner Porter Wagoner was so horrified that he urged her not to release it: she did, and it was summarily banned by country radio.

And behind her image, she could be a model of smart, steely self-determination. If the country music establishment had a tendency to look down on her (the songwriter Tom T Hall once noted that he and Kris Kristofferson were the only two people in Nashville “who could describe Dolly Parton without using their hands”), she was abundantly aware of her own worth. The then-more-famous Wagoner was doing her a favour in 1967 when he adopted her as his duet partner, but Parton did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the pair’s songwriting, and left when it became apparent her success was beginning to outstrip his, occasioning a $3m lawsuit in the process. Moreover, she famously turned down Elvis Presley’s overtures to record the heart-rending song she wrote about the duo’s split, I Will Always Love You, when Presley’s manager indicated he wanted a cut of the songwriting royalties in return.

She was clearly possessed of a far greater artistic and commercial ambition than she was given credit for. The former was evidenced by 1973’s My Tennessee Mountain Home, an entirely self-penned autobiographical concept album that was rather less sentimental in its recollections than you might expect: “No amount of money could pay me to go back and live through it again,” she sang of her poverty-stricken rural upbringing on In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). It ranks among the best things she ever released. Her daring became apparent around the time of the Walters interview, when Parton made a lunge for the pop mainstream, disregarding fears that it would alienate her existing audience.

She scored a succession of huge pop hits: 1977’s Mann and Weill-penned Here You Come Again went to No 3 on the Hot 100, a chart on which Jolene had, incredibly, only peaked at No 60; three years later 9 to 5 hit No 1. She also transformed into an actor and dabbled in disco without losing her country essence. During her quest for mainstream success, she was as likely to essay a bluegrass version of the Beatles’ Help!, or a cover of Woody Guthrie’s Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos), or unleash upon the world Me and Little Andy, a song that anywhere other than Nashville would be regarded as a bit much – a child and a puppy snuff it in the final verse – as she was to release the winningly high-camp disco of Potential New Boyfriend. She really did know exactly what she was doing.

In a sense, her moment as a mainstream crossover pop star was relatively short-lived. There was one more huge hit with 1983’s peerless Islands in the Stream, a Bee Gees-penned duet with Kenny Rodgers, but that moment had drawn to close by the time of 1987’s Rainbow. It seemed Parton had reached her limit with trying to cater to a broad audience – doggedly ploughing her way through its written-to-order contents, she sounded bored stiff, particularly when compared with the same year’s superb Trio, a collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt.

And besides, Rainbow’s commercial failure didn’t matter. Perhaps because she had never really turned her back on country – 1984’s Tennessee Homesick Blues opened with sound of Parton yodelling – Nashville welcomed her full-blooded return to the genre, with 1989’s Ricky Skaggs-produced White Limozeen. If she never scored another US Hot 100 hit, the broader celebrity she had established in the late 70s and early 80s never waned for the rest of her life. Tellingly, while promoting White Limozeen’s standout track, the insanely catchy and uproariously funny Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That?, she hosted Saturday Night Live: it would be a decade before another country star did so.

In truth, Parton’s subsequent albums were of a decidedly mixed quality, at least until she returned to absolute basics: 1999’s Grammy-winning The Grass Is Blue kicked off a trio of stark, fantastic albums that dealt in bluegrass, Appalachian folk and country gospel, the music that she had “grown up surrounded by”. Thereafter, what she put out was hit-and-and miss: misjudged horrors including 2003’s post-9/11 collection of patriotic songs, For God and Country, abutting albums as good as 2014’s Blue Smoke, although her voice sounded magnificent no matter the material. She was still more than capable of writing fantastic songs – but nothing that could eclipse the best of her 70s material.

It didn’t really matter, because the best of her 70s material had long taken on a life of its own outside country music. Whitney Houston’s cover of I Will Always Love You became the biggest-selling single of all time by a female artist. At the last count, Jolene has been covered nearly 90 times: you could hear it rendered as noisy alt-rock by the White Stripes, synth-pop by Strawberry Switchblade, or a dubby post-club soundtrack by One Dove. Stars queued up to pay homage.

Meanwhile, in the 21st century, the full extent of Parton’s influence on pop became apparent. Younger stars queued up to pay homage of one kind or another. Taylor Swift, who knows a thing or two about pivoting away from country to pop, called her “a force of evolution and transformation in our industry”. Parton co-wrote Rainbowland on her goddaughter Miley Cyrus’s 2017 album Younger Now, and you didn’t have to analyse Sabrina Carpenter’s work too deeply to spot the influence. The fact that Carpenter’s 2024 smash Please Please Please sounded like something Parton might have written evidently didn’t escape Parton herself: she turned up duetting with Carpenter on a remixed version of the song, the swearing decorously omitted.

As fans of Tammy Wynette or Patsy Cline would be quick to point out, Parton certainly wasn’t the first female country star to cross over into the pop charts, but she nevertheless seemed like the godmother of the pop-country that has swept the charts in recent years, which one Spotify playlist characterised as “Neon Cowgirl” (Parton was by far the oldest artist to make said playlist, rubbing shoulders with Swift, Carpenter, Chappell Roan, Kesha et al). When Beyoncé made a musical leap into country on Cowboy Carter, it somehow seemed inevitable that Parton would be involved, and so it proved: she delivered a spoken-word introduction to Beyoncé’s redux of Jolene. In fact, she seemed as present in pop music in the mid-2020s as she had been in the late 70s. The difference was that no one would have asked her if she was a joke. That question had been answered to everyone’s satisfaction a long time ago.

Dolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 17:59:40 GMT

Songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 also invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causes

Alexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career which turned country music cliches inside out

Dolly Parton – a life in pictures

Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updates

Share your tributes and memories of Dolly Parton

Dolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80.

Her death was announced by nephew Brian Seaver on Instagram. “I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now,” he said. “It is an honour, an honour that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness.”

So gifted that she wrote two of the 20th century’s greatest songs – Jolene and I Will Always Love You – in a single day, Parton’s songwriting was characterised by its vivid storytelling, emotional acuity and melodic strength, all sung with strident clarity. From an eventual catalogue of hundreds of songs, she scored a record 25 US country No 1 singles and 47 albums in the country Top 10 . She crossed over into the pop charts with 9 to 5, a US No 1 in 1980; balanced her music career with acclaimed acting, twice earning Golden Globe nominations for her roles; and her Imagination Library literacy scheme donated more than 150m books to children.

This was all done with considerable panache, rhinestoned glamour and towering hairdos, with her immortal assertion regarding her appearance – “it takes a lot of money to look this cheap” – the most quoted example of Parton’s ready wit.

Parton was born in poverty in a one-room cabin in Tennessee, the fourth child to a mother who would have 12 children by the age of 35, and a father who was a farmer and construction worker. One of her best-loved songs, Coat of Many Colours, was about her mother creating patchwork clothes; Parton’s first guitar was cobbled together from a mandolin with bass guitar strings. Her first proper guitar was given to her aged eight by her uncle, and she went from singing in church, to appearing on local television aged 10, to cutting her first record aged 13. That year she appeared at the Grand Ole Opry, the concert hall in Nashville at the centre of country music, and her performance was introduced by Johnny Cash. “I’ve always believed things would go well, and I dreamed that they would even before I was in high school,” she later said. “I always wanted to be a star. It just seemed natural to me.”

After graduating high school in 1964 she moved to Nashville and started out as a songwriter rather than performer. The following year she was signed as an artist and initially moulded as a pop singer, without success; after she was allowed to switch to country, she scored back-to-back hits and released her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly. In 1966 she married Carl Dean – who died in 2025, with the couple renewing their vows in 2016 to mark 50 years together.

Beginning in 1967, a duet partnership with country singer and TV personality Porter Wagoner helped her star continue to ascend, and she had her first country No 1 in 1971 with the song Joshua.

Jolene, her unforgettably raw and desperate plea to a rival lover, was released in 1973 and became her first UK success, reaching No 7. I Will Always Love You, written to Wagoner as a farewell after their creative partnership, was a country No 1 in 1974 and again via a re-recorded version in 1982, and would go on to be a huge pop success when revived by Whitney Houston for the soundtrack of The Bodyguard in 1992: it is still the bestselling single of all time by a woman, with an estimated 20m sales.

In the mid 1970s Parton broadened her sound, embracing pop-rock arrangements on songs such as 1977’s Light of a Clear Blue Morning – its accompanying album New Harvest … First Gathering was her first entry in the pop album chart. Later that year its follow-up Here You Come Again reached the Top 20 and was her first million-selling LP, powered in part by its hit title track, which also won Parton the first of her 10 Grammy awards.

1980 was a peak in her success, with three back-to-back country No 1s, including 9 to 5, taken from the film of the same name which Parton starred in alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, earning her an Oscar nomination for best original song. Parton would later write songs for a stage musical version of 9 to 5, in 2008.

Another classic single came in 1983: Islands in the Stream, a duet with Kenny Rogers, which topped the US pop charts, and a Christmas album with Rogers in 1984 went two times platinum. There were more notable film roles in the 1980s, too, opposite Burt Reynolds in the The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, Sylvester Stallone in Rhinestone, and an all-star female ensemble in Steel Magnolias.

Sign up to Breaking News US

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

A landmark Parton album came in 1987 with Trio, an exquisitely harmonised, springwater-clear collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, earning Parton her only nomination for album of the year at the Grammys. Another all-star trio recording came in 1993, with Tammy Wynette and Loretta Lynn on the album Honky-Tonk Angels, followed by a reunion with Harris and Ronstadt for Trio II in 1999, featuring a Grammy-winning cover of Neil Young’s After the Gold Rush.

The turn of the century brought a trilogy of acclaimed bluegrass albums, and Parton would release 10 more LPs, the most recent being Rockstar in 2023. She was courted by a younger generation of stars, appearing with country artists such as Brad Paisley as well as pop singers such as Kesha, and her goddaughter Miley Cyrus. There were fewer acting roles, but she lent her voice to animated film Gnomeo and Juliet in 2011 and the following year appeared alongside Queen Latifah and more in the musical film Joyful Noise.

Alongside her music and acting, Parton was an astute businesswoman and philanthropist. She founded the film and TV production company Sandollar, with former manager Sandy Gallin, which went on to produce hits such as Buffy the Vampire Slayer and the Father of the Bride film series. In 1986, she took a stake in the Silver Dollar City theme park in Tennessee and renamed it Dollywood, doubling its size over the next two decades, and a Dollywood-branded spa, cabin complex, theatre-restaurant concept and waterpark have since been opened.

The Dollywood Foundation, funded through these business ventures and creative projects, was created in 1988, initially awarding college scholarships and running a scheme to help children complete high school in her native Sevier County, Tennessee. In 1995 Parton began her Imagination Library project, which sent an age-appropriate book to every child in the county every month until they were five. “My father could not read and write, and I saw how crippling that could be,” she explained. It expanded nationwide in 2000, internationally in 2006, and nearly 25m books are now distributed each year across the US, Canada, Australia, the UK and Ireland.

In 2022, Jeff Bezos donated $100m (£83m) to the foundation. That year, Parton explained that as well as improving child literacy, “it’s the fact they get recognised. They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special. They start taking pride in themselves, and they know that somebody out there is thinking of [them].”

Parton has also set up a reserve in 2003 to help preserve the bald eagle; contributed $500,000 to the opening of a Sevier county hospital in 2006; coordinated relief efforts for those affected by the Smoky mountain wildfires of 2016; and contributed to an HIV/Aids charity album. She supported Black Lives Matter and transgender rights, opposing a North Carolina “bathroom bill” that restricted transgender people’s access to toilets (Parton was also nominated for an Oscar for her song in trans drama Transamerica, entitled Travelin’ Thru).

She made a number of donations to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, where her niece was treated for leukaemia. The most high profile of these was in 2020, when she donated $1m for research into Covid-19, which formed the basis for the eventual Moderna vaccine.

In May 2026, Parton cancelled her Las Vegas residency over health issues. A Broadway musical is also set to open later this year after a run in Nashville.

The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 17:27:24 GMT

Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home

Three moves in the last week have exposed the limits of Donald Trump’s economic bullying. The US slapped 50% tariffs on another $20bn of Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on the cars, trucks, parts and steel that America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs and pro-billionaire tax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasury stepped in to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it.

The Trump administration’s “D-day” sanctions are potentially the most consequential because they expose the scaffolding of American financial power. While markets shrugged off the immediate threat, that calculation might change were the US to target a major Chinese refinery or bank. Such an escalation could spark a trade war with Beijing. The US has leverage. But China has pressure points – especially farmers in Republican states – that make using it costly. In the long run, there is a price to pay. Nations hold one another’s currencies partly because they trust the political relationship. Mr Trump is testing what happens when they don’t.

The moves to control the bond market are the most revealing. There is nothing new about Washington managing yields: the Federal Reserve has long been able to buy treasuries. What is new is Mr Bessent doing it so openly to deal with the fallout from failed policies. Mr Trump owns this: his tariffs raise input costs; his Iran war pushed up energy costs; his nonchalance about rising American grocery prices reassures no one. When that mixture helps produce higher inflation expectations and rising long-end bond yields, Mr Trump’s team steps in to prevent interest rates ticking up.

The US president is willing to use state power to lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes. Mr Bessent wants to stop rising long yields feeding into investment and Washington’s debt-interest bill. That his former mentor at George Soros’s hedge fund criticises him and wants bond markets to force spending cuts is not to be applauded. The better question for Mr Bessent is: why shield markets from the consequences of Mr Trump’s acts, but not households?

The trade war with Canada is economically stupid and legally dubious. In 2025, the Trump tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per US household. More than a quarter of Canadian exports to the US are now subject to significant tariffs or threatened with tougher ones. Ottawa’s retaliation will start in September. North American production has been organised around such trade flows and tariffs will make US manufacturing more expensive, not less.

Why Canada? Washington has largely given up trying to change China’s economic model. Canada is seen as a soft target. The Guardian columnist Robert Reich is surely right: Mr Trump picks on a friendly neighbour because that is what bullies do. This cannot go on. American economic power depends on other countries wanting to remain in a system the US dominates. Mr Trump thinks their dependence is his weapon. The more often he uses it against them, the harder they should look for the exit.

The Guardian view on the French left: division makes Marine Le Pen’s path to the Élysée more straightforward

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 17:27:03 GMT

Two years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missing

In the summer of 2024, as polls suggested that Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National party would win a snap legislative election rashly called by Emmanuel Macron, the perennially fragmented French left united to spectacular effect. The New Popular Front, whose name evoked Léon Blum’s anti-fascist alliance in the 1930s, came first in a poll that delivered a hung parliament.

Eight months before a presidential contest in which Ms Le Pen is the clear frontrunner, the prospect of a repeat performance appears close to zero. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed, and Olivier Faure, the leader of the Socialist party (PS), have both ruled out the idea of backing a single candidate. Efforts by the Greens to broker talks between progressive parties have fallen on deaf ears.

The obvious danger, as the most important election in the history of the Fifth Republic looms, is that chronic division will ease Ms Le Pen’s path to the Élysée. The 75-year-old Mr Mélenchon is a deeply polarising figure who has failed three times to reach the second round of a presidential race. But in a fractured field, the loyalty of his base among the young, the urban precariat and ethnic minority voters gives him a credible chance of making the runoff this time. At which point, polls predict, France’s traditional “Republican front” against the far right would disintegrate, handing Ms Le Pen a crushing victory.

Within the PS, the picture is one of confusion and debilitating internal rivalries. Raphael Glucksmann, the leader of Public Square, a small sister movement, declared his candidacy on Sunday and is favourite to win a joint primary. But senior figures such as the former president François Hollande are rumoured to be waiting to make their own move later on. The Greens are divided over whether to offer support to Mr Mélenchon’s uncompromising leftism and reward his new emphasis on the environment, or back Mr Glucksmann’s more centrist strategy.

All of which makes Mr Glucksmann’s stated ambition to “rebuild the left” seem somewhat optimistic. A Parisian intellectual married to a famous television newsreader (who has taken leave for the duration of the campaign), he is polling at 10% and is unburdened by the aura of failure that has dogged the Socialist party in recent years. But if he becomes its presidential candidate, he will face the same challenge as his immediate predecessors: how to reconnect with alienated blue-collar towns that now vote for Ms Le Pen, while simultaneously courting Mr Mélenchon’s urban radicals and reassuring middle-class voters who deserted for Mr Macron.

In 2022, the former Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo comprehensively flunked that test, receiving 1.75% of votes cast. A historic humiliation was partly the result of progressive voters calculating that Mr Mélenchon was the left candidate with the best chance of coming second, thus excluding Ms Le Pen from the runoff. But as the 2027 campaign begins in earnest, she enjoys a 20-point lead in the polls, and another place in the second round is all but assured.

The question, therefore, is who can rally enough support from across the political spectrum to stop her becoming president. A united left would have had a far better chance of coming up with a convincing answer. But that is not the left France currently has.

‘They make life much easier’: AI-powered shopping trolleys go on trial in Lancashire

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 17:14:34 GMT

Customers give their verdicts as a Morrisons store becomes the first the UK to test trolleys that scan, weigh and tally costs

Lancashire has been the site of many British innovations throughout history, from the spinning jenny, which transformed textile production, to the creation of jelly babies.

Now it has welcomed another first: AI shopping trolleys.

A Morrisons in Lancashire has become the first supermarket in the UK to trial the use of “smart trolleys” that allow customers to do their shopping without having to scan a single item.

The AI-powered Caper smart trolleys, created by San Francisco-based Instacart, automatically register each item placed in the trolley, adding up the cost and recommending related products as you shop. Once finished, customers can scan their trolley screen rather than visiting a checkout.

Preston is the first city in Britain to use them after the supermarket chain announced a deal to trial them at its location in Ashton-on-Ribble, to the west of the city.

Amazon Fresh, which allowed shoppers to take items from the shelves and leave the shop without checking out, using cameras to charge directly to online accounts, failed to take off in the UK, with the company’s last physical British store closing in 2025. But Morrisons is more hopeful that its smart trolleys will be a success, with plans to put them in supermarkets across the country.

The smart trolleys are already used in more than 100 cities across the world. They are similar in design and function to the Dash Cart used by Amazon’s Fresh stores, which still operate outside the UK.

After the trolleys rolled into Ashton-on-Ribble last month, customer Matthew Byrne said they had “massively” helped him keep track of his shopping. Byrne is autistic and struggles to stick to set plans for what to get from the shops.

“Having what I’ve bought on screen has been great. I have a habit of just grabbing things and throwing them in my trolley, and then wondering how I’m paying so much. It’s been amazing to visualise it and see it in real time. I came here with an £80 budget, and I’ve actually been able to stick to it.”

Kaz Bond was disappointed to be forced to use a normal trolley for her latest shop due to a fault on her phone, having used them for every trip she has made to Morrisons since they became commonplace around four weeks ago.

“Honestly, I think they’re brilliant,” said Bond. “They make life much easier. I wouldn’t be that surprised if they’re everywhere before long. I reckon it’s the future.”

Debbie Files had chosen Tuesday as the day to take a leap of faith and use the trolleys for the first time, albeit with the help of a Morrisons employee.

“It was a little bit confusing at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly,” said Files. “It’s heavy, though. I’ve barely been able to turn it. I feel like I need a driving lesson to use it, but I got the hang of it. If they make a smaller one then that will get me to use it again.”

Community-maxxing: gen Z are done with doomscrolling – and ready to socialise

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 16:59:55 GMT

Research shows young adults often feel isolated. So alongside embracing ‘grandma hobbies’, they want to get involved with the places they live and be good neighbours

Name: Community-maxxing.

Age: The portmanteau is recent, but Homo sapiens have always been social creatures.

Appearance: Cosily communal.

Community-maxxing? But I thought I was supposed to be solo-maxxing! Well, that means being single, so you could do both.

Explain. Community-maxxing is seeking out regular in-person connections around you, often tied to shared interests. Vice reports that gen Z are “done doomscrolling” and are getting out in the world, sharing their passions, interests and “grandma hobbies” with like-minded folk by joining book groups, crafting circles, hiking and run clubs.

You’re telling me gen Z have invented socialising? There’s more to it than that. Community-maxxing is also being a good neighbour, feeling part of the place you live in and being open to new connections.

Can you give an example? At this summer’s Boomtown festival in the West Country, a group of Bristolian festival-goers welcomed Adam James, a young autistic fellow raver, who was attending his first festival alone, into their group for three days. They unquestioningly accepted James, giving him what he described as the best weekend of his life. “It’s what the community’s about, really,” James said.

OK, that’s lovely. Good on gen Z. Community-maxxing is a way of combating loneliness and digitally enabled isolation, which are really problematic for their generation. “On an average day in 2023 one in 10 US young adults did not spend a single minute interacting face-to-face with another person,” the Financial Times reported earlier this month. Over here, Office for National Statistics research published last November found 33% of 16- to 29-year-olds felt lonely “often, always or some of the time”.

That’s bleak – no wonder they’re craving connection. Yes, humans are social creatures – we need each other. “Community-maxxing … has become an accepted term in recent years to describe what therapists have known for decades: that individuals require repeated, quality social interaction to assist in developing a feeling of grounding and support,” therapist Stephanie Lewis told Vice.

That’s true of everyone, surely, not just the youth. Yes, community-maxxing isn’t just for kids. You might have noticed there’s a renewed interest in communal living these days, from multi-generational shared spaces to co-housing projects and communities for older people.

Hmm, I don’t think I’m up for joining a commune: I’m very particular about my towels. You can community-maxx however you like, in big or small ways. Suggestions online include “ask to borrow a tool instead of buying one”, “become a regular volunteer” and “chat to the person sitting next to you at your local cafe”. You could join a choir! Fix stuff at your local repair cafe!

Fine, but I still hate the word. How about IRL-core, community-coded, going social-mode, or people-pilled? We could get a group together in a nice local cafe to workshop this.

Do say: “Gen Z are realising it takes a village to be a happy, fulfilled human.”

Don’t say: “Sorry I missed pottery club – I’m solo-maxxing, so no one woke me after sleep-maxxing, and after fibremaxxing, skin-maxxing and gym-maxxing, I was so tired I sleep-maxxed again.”

There’s no place like a revered writer’s home

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 16:44:35 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial on preserving the homes of writers such as William Blake, Ted Hughes and William Wordsworth for the public

Your editorial (The Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s own, 18 August) rightly laments that George Eliot has no publicly open home despite efforts to secure one. The same is true, remarkably, of William Blake, and he is at least as worthy a cause, and arguably even more influential.

Poet, painter, printmaker and author of the words behind Jerusalem, Blake has no open home anywhere. Of his nine addresses, only two survive. In London, the apartment he rented is disappearing behind new development. The other, his cottage in Felpham, West Sussex, where he and his wife, Catherine, lived from 1800 to 1803 and experienced an outburst of creativity, is the only one that could ever open to the public.

I am a trustee of the Blake Cottage Trust, which has spent two years saving it. In 2024 the roof was near collapse and the cottage was on Historic England’s at-risk register. Thanks to The National Lottery Heritage Fund and other foundations, artisans have rebuilt the roof and removed a Victorian extension, returning the cottage to its original form. But much of the fabric still needs full conservation before the cottage is truly saved and can be opened to all, and that work costs a great deal of money.

Raising it has not been easy. Even with the backing of the Heritage Fund and other trusts, we will need private philanthropy to fill a significant gap – and, as your article notes of Rydal Mount, heritage sites live or die on relevance and sustainability as much as repair.

That’s why our ambition goes beyond bricks and thatch to include opening an arts and education centre near the cottage, conceived not just as somewhere to visit but as a living place of creativity and inspiration in its own right – one with year-round appeal for the local community as much as for returning visitors, and one that properly honours Catherine Blake too, who learned to read under William’s guidance and helped hand-print and colour the plates of his illuminated books.

With the 2027 bicentenary of Blake’s death approaching, this is a moment when Guardian readers could make a real difference – to find out more, visit blakecottage. orgRichard ClemmowTrustee, The Blake Cottage Trust

Your editorial gave a commendable overview of the important work that writers’ houses and museums have been doing to reconnect us with our literary heritage. Of course, turning a writer’s house into a museum is difficult, and not always viable. But this needn’t mean that the house cannot be saved for the nation and enjoyed by the public.

The late poet laureate Ted Hughes was born in a tiny end-terrace house in Mytholmroyd, West Yorkshire. He claimed his first years there “shaped everything”. But the house is too small to accommodate tour groups (who would inevitably inconvenience the neighbours), and parking is limited to just a space or two on a residential street. So, when the house was saved 20 years ago by The Elmet Trust, a local charity, it was opened to paying guests as a holiday cottage or writer’s retreat.

This fully immersive experience goes beyond a visit to any museum. It places you in the poet’s shoes. Sleeping in the cosy attic room that Hughes shared with his older brother, or in the bedroom where he was born, inspires because it impresses upon us how humble his start in life was. Leaflets guide you to his favourite walks through the glorious Yorkshire woods and hillsides where he played as a child. His writings often described these places, or the views from his windows, and indeed the rooms in the house itself. There are no display cases, no text panels in sight. This is about lived experience.

A George Eliot museum is indeed a worthy aspiration; a Ted Hughes museum scarcely less so. Yet while a museum is a fitting tribute to any great author, literary tourism at its best is about the readers and the fans as much as the writers. Interactive visitor centres such as Seamus Heaney HomePlace are as vital a part of the future as traditional museums. Engaging with literary landscapes and walks is no less important – for health, for wellbeing, for our environment, for our imaginations. But surely nothing can beat stepping inside the world of a writer by staying in their home, for which, as Genevieve Fox reported in a Guardian travel article in 2021, the range of options is surprisingly large. Dr David RudrumSecretary, The Elmet Trust

Along with Rydal Mount and Dove Cottage, William Wordsworth also lived in two other Cumbrian houses which are open to the public. His childhood home, Wordsworth House in Cockermouth, owned by the National Trust, is currently only open for organised tours. The National Trust blames financial losses and low visitor numbers since the pandemic. Allan Bank in Grasmere, where Wordsworth lived briefly, is also owned by the National Trust, and open five days a week.

But Rydal Mount was considered by Wordsworth to be his favourite home, and it’s where he lived for most of his life, until his death in 1850. I spent several years working for the Wordsworth family and curators, and the house has a fascinating history as well as a glorious location and exciting future. Wordsworth himself was only a tenant; the house was eventually bought by the family – his great-great-granddaughter Mary Henderson acquired it in 1969.

Since then it’s seen the development of the five-acre gardens to plans drawn up by the poet. It has staged drama, music and poetry, co-hosted a film festival with the local cinema, and hosted weddings – including that of the poet’s great-great-great-great grandson Christopher Andrew. There was even, in the 1970s, a performance by the dance troupe Pan’s People when Miss UK contestants were filmed there.

It will be exciting to see how the Wordsworth Trust, which acquired Rydal Mount in March, takes the life of the house forward. The challenge is to re-engage visitors with the life and work of the greatest of the Romantic poets, and poetry generally. The Wordsworth family initiated a successful poetry competition for Cumbrian school pupils and planned to roll this out nationwide. Perhaps that will bring a new generation to appreciate more than just Daffodils. Eileen JonesAuthor of Rydal Mount: The Story of Wordsworth’s Home

Why the threat from the rampaging AI machine went ignored

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 16:44:28 GMT

Jonathan Michie on his father’s efforts in the 1970s to map out concerns regarding widespread social coercion driven by automation. Plus a letter from Callum Brown

Jill Lepore asks why nobody listened to warnings about the threats posed from the AI revolution (Democracy v the machine, 18 August). As she is a Harvard professor, her piece is understandably US-centric. But in 1972 there was an international gathering of AI researchers and others in Italy to tackle the ethical and social implications of AI.

This “Serbelloni group” of global experts (they met at Villa Serbelloni on Lake Como) was led by my father, Donald Michie, the director of the University of Edinburgh’s department of machine intelligence. The group mapped out early concerns regarding potential political tyranny, the erosion of human autonomy and widespread social coercion driven by automation.

Why did nobody listen? In part because the next year the UK cut research funding for machine learning, robotics and AI, following the Lighthill report, which had been established – it has since been documented – for this purpose. Researchers had instead to focus on more immediately industrial-relevant work. My father’s attempts to reconvene the Serbelloni group to include experts from the humanities thus proved unsuccessful. Jonathan MichieProfessor of innovation & knowledge exchange, University of Oxford

Jill Lepore rightly traces those welcoming the rampaging AI machine in a free market while modern humanists fear the unchecked machine. She mentions the underestimated American intellectual Lewis Mumford, who devoted most of his life to restraining the uninhibited city as a form of machine damaging people by the million. He hooked up with the British humanist Frederic J Osborn in a letter exchange that lasted over three decades, developing a sane town-planning system.

Mumford was wise enough to see that the automatic machine had the capacity to make man passive and purposeless in the same manner as did living in the city, and humans must resist induced passivity of all kinds. So the myth still prevails. Beware – AI is really not that smart, and a few well-chosen puzzles for it to solve expose its crippling obsession with data, not with the humans’ forte, knowledge. Callum BrownProfessor emeritus in history, University of Glasgow

Reading Katriona O’Sullivan’s article (Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me, 19 August) reminded me of when I was a community worker at the Park Hill estate in Sheffield in the 1970s.

When I (young and naive) asked the mums why they bought chips for their toddlers for lunch rather than spending the money on fresh fruit (I cringe now in embarrassment), they pointed out that a bag of chips was the price of a couple of apples and one of them filled the kids up. I began to understand, and to also see why they spent money on cigarettes. As O’Sullivan says, “a few bottles [of alcohol] can feel like an escape”.

My work there gave me a lifetime of experience in a few months, which I’ve never forgotten. Carol TaylorMatlock, Derbyshire

What an excellent piece by Katriona O’Sullivan – a very timely riposte to those who pass judgment from the comfort of their broadcasting pods. George Orwell made similar points in The Road to Wigan Pier – desperately poor people still tried (occasionally) to go to the cinema or buy ice-cream rather than spend their subsistence national assistance on tripe.

It was – and is – a matter of human dignity and feeling that you are still living as a person, not as an automaton, as more fortunate people might expect you to be. Perhaps cheap toothbrushes should be free to our poorest citizens as a sensible public-health intervention. Howard WilliamsonTreforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf

US politics live – latest updates

Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US.

In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices.

The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year.

The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House.

The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9m) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper.

The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US.

In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”.

The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war.

“You have power,” she said.

The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months.

Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around.

Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US.

Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”

Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”.

Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

People’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it?

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 16:00:18 GMT

Discussing people’s bodies can be fraught. We asked eating disorder experts how to do so – or not – responsibly

In the age of Ozempic and people being open about plastic surgery, discussion about people’s bodies is rife. At the same time, nobody seems quite sure how to talk about them, as shown by recent coverage of celebrities like Ariana Grande.

It is a fraught topic. We asked eating disorder experts for guidelines to follow when talking about other people’s bodies, and how to do so without doing harm.

For experts in the field of eating disorders, the current ambivalence makes sense. “There’s a whiplash moment we’re stuck in,” says Dr Tom Hildebrandt, director of the Center for Eating and Weight Disorders at Mount Sinai hospital in New York.

The body positivity movement of the 2010s saw a mainstream push to “accept all body sizes, shapes and types”, says Hildebrandt. Then, with the explosion of GLP-1s, progress toward body acceptance “took a hard right turn”, he says – once again, “the media went through its idealization of weight loss”.

The vocabulary is different than it was before. Now, the focus is on “optimizing” one’s body and appearance, says Dr Ulrike Schmidt, professor of eating disorders at King’s College London.

The deluge of social media posts has only exacerbated the confusion and made it feel impossible to escape body discourse.

“The internet, specifically social media, has made commentary on the appearance of others more visible and widespread,” says Jessica Scheer, CEO of the National Eating Disorders Association (Neda). “Most of the commentary is speculative, and almost all of it is harmful.”

“Everything is about context,” says Hildebrandt. “It means something different in your physician’s office than it does on a social media account for the whole world to see.”

When considering how or whether to discuss bodies with other people, keep in mind that many people are unhappy with their bodies and appearance, says Schmidt. She points to a 2023 report by the Butterfly Foundation, Australia’s national charity for eating disorders and body image issues, which found that 57% of young people were dissatisfied with how they look, and 49% said this had sometimes stopped them from attending school.

“Even the seemingly most innocent and well-meaning comments about people’s body weight, shape or appearance have the potential for backfiring, sensitizing or hurting people,” she says. In her work as an eating disorder clinician, Schmidt says many of the people she sees recall comments about their bodies as the starting point of their eating disorder journey. Some of these comments were criticisms or warnings about changing bodies, while others were intended as compliments.

“In clinic, we often hear that these kinds of congratulatory comments … made them think they are only acceptable, attractive and desirable if they are a certain weight or physique,” Schmidt says.

Body talk is ubiquitous, and it can be difficult not to engage. We asked experts how one might respond in various contexts.

If an acquaintance or colleague brings up another person or celebrity’s body: When someone you aren’t very close to engages in body talk, you may not want to get involved. Often, discussing people’s bodies can be like talking about the weather, Hildebrandt says – a topic one turns to when there is nothing else to talk about. “But it’s a very low-level social connection; it doesn’t have much meaning to it.”

In most cases, he says, people’s remarks about others’ bodies are not badly meant. They are more like a reflex, something we have been conditioned to believe is acceptable small talk. “I tell people to be bored by it,” says Hildebrandt. As soon as you signal that you’re not interested – by not engaging and changing the topic, for example – people will move on quickly,” Hildebrandt says.

(Experts have noted that this is also a useful strategy if you feel activated by other people’s discussion of body shapes and sizes.)

If a child criticizes their body or someone else’s: “If a young child says something negative about their body, it might be helpful to ask: ‘What makes you say that?’” says Schmidt.

They might have made the comment because they are being bullied or teased by other children, or because they are mirroring the comments of an adult. “Depending on the origins of the comment, the response may need to be quite different,” Schmidt says.

Hildebrandt tells his own children that public discussion of people’s bodies is “just trying to get your attention” and often features “lazy” messaging.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“If someone’s going to try to sell me something based on somebody’s body type, they’re being lazy,” he says. “They’re just assigning a body value to get your attention.”

The antidote, he says – in these conversations and in general – is to actively pursue other interests. It’s tough to simply “be less interested” in this prevalent topic, he says; “you have to be more interested in something else.”

If an older relative criticizes or praises someone’s body: We may technically speak the same language as older relatives, but we may not always mean the same thing, Hildebrandt notes. For example, when you say “phone”, you mean a smartphone; “for your grandparents, it’s something that hangs on the wall.”

This same language mismatch can happen in discussions about bodies. A grandparent’s remark about another person’s weight loss may be a comment about their overall success or an expression of concern about their wellbeing. Hildebrandt argues that it is more helpful to engage with their intended meaning as opposed to being overly literal and “ending up in a situation where there’s friction”.

If people are discussing someone’s body on social media: Experts say it’s best not to comment in these public forums.

“I see a lot of talk online about the harms of staying silent,” says Scheer. “However, making speculative comments about a person’s weight or physical appearance is not the antidote to silence.”

In instances where a publicly speculated eating disorder may be the case, she says, “critical online discourse may be the digital reinforcement that fuels their continued behavior”.

Is there ever a time when posting about someone else’s body on social media is valuable? “I haven’t heard of one yet,” says Hildebrandt.

If you are struggling with seeing body discussions on social media, Neda recommends, among other things, limiting screen time and thinking critically about the media we are exposed to, including asking questions like: “Who created and profits from the message?”

If you are worried about a friend or close relative: Speculating about a stranger’s health and worrying about a friend are two very different things. If you have concerns about a friend’s body image or eating behavior, experts recommend being direct and compassionate.

“Be inquisitive, honest and open,” says Hildebrandt. “Don’t jump to a solution. Most people don’t want solutions – certainly not right off the bat. They want to be heard and understood, so being open and curious will get you the furthest.”

Scheer also suggests focusing the conversation not on a person’s appearance, “but the other aspects that generally accompany an eating disorder, like social isolation and brain fog”.

“None of us have the ability to control other people,” says Hildebrandt. “The other person is going to dictate whether the conversation goes further or not. If you’ve demonstrated that you can listen, hear and understand, then chances are you’re going to have more conversations.”

“We had a long talk about it, and it was a hard decision for her,” Mulkey continued. “I know it is hard because she loves LSU. Kate is a great person. She has to do what she feels is right for her, and we fully support her in that. We all wish her the best.”

Koval, who was born in Kyiv and whose father serves in the Ukrainian military, began her college career at Notre Dame. She transferred before last season to LSU, where she averaged 8.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 16.6 minutes per game. Koval played high school basketball in New York, where she was one of the best young players in the country, and represented Ukraine at the Fiba 3x3 World Cup this summer.

Earlier this month, LSU signed Anna Minaeva, a 17-year-old who previously played professionally with MBA Moscow.

In an interview with the Times-Picayune/New Orleans Advocate last week, Mulkey said she had spoken to Koval about Minaeva joining the team before the signing was announced.

“I want you to understand I’m not here to ask you to change how you feel about Russia,” Mulkey recalled telling Koval. “I’m just here out of respect for your family and out of respect for you to let you know. Because I know how personal it is for you. Know that what I have to do in this business, I cannot make a decision to not recruit somebody that can help our program because of a conflict between two countries.”

Mulkey had said she hoped the two players could be “ambassadors” for sport and peace amid the conflict.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the two countries have been at war since.
