Prime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy Boston

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 15:26:38 GMT

Boston was one of the finest players in the sport’s history

Wigan plan series of tributes in Thursday’s Hull KR clash

Andy ­Burnham says he is “heart­broken” by the death of Sir Billy ­Boston after the prime minister led tri­butes to the rugby league icon.

Boston died on Tuesday at the age of 92. He was one of the sport’s all‑time great players, scoring almost 500 tries during an illustrious career for Wigan Warriors and Great Britain, and last year became the first man in rugby league history to be knighted for his services to the game.

His death comes just four days after the funeral of his wife of more than 70 years, Lady Joan Boston, who died last month. Burnham, a lifelong rugby league supporter who also served as president of the Rugby Football League, described Boston as a “giant of a man in every way”.

The prime minister wrote: “Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died. Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.

“He always had time for people and gave so much back to his adopted home, Wigan. I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy’s ­family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan. A giant of a man in every way. Thank you, Billy, and rest in peace.”

Boston joined Wigan in 1953 after starting his rugby career in his native Wales. He went on to score 478 tries in 488 games for the club, winning a plethora of honours for club and country. Only one man, the Warring­ton winger Brian Bevan, has more tries in the history of the sport than Boston.

Less than a year after leaving Wales to begin a career in league, Boston became the first non-white player to be selected for Great Britain. He scored 36 tries in 18 games on that tour to Australia and New Zealand in 1954, and was part of the Lions’ World Cup-winning squad of 1960.

Boston was awarded an MBE in 1996 but, last year, he became the first rugby league player to be knighted for services to the sport. That accolade was met with emotional ­celebrations in Wigan, the town in which he remained after retirement and where one of three statues – alongside those at Wembley and Cardiff – stands ­fea­turing Boston, which underlines his life and career.

The Warriors are planning for an emotional occasion on Thursday evening when they host Hull KR in Super League, with a series of ­tributes planned to celebrate Boston’s life. Their head coach, Matt Peet, paid an emotional tribute on Tuesday while conducting his pre-match press duties. “It’s like he was on a different planet, really,” Peet said of Boston’s career.

“I wish I could see more of him. I’ve seen bits of footage, but I think it’s more the legend when people talk about him in terms of the ­stories and players that played against him, ­players that played with him. It’s going to be a real tribute night on Thursday.

Obviously, people are very upset and rightly so, but you’ve got to celebrate a life well lived. Everything that Billy represented and stood for.

We have a responsibility to uphold the whole history of the club when you work at a club like this, but I think Billy’s top of the tree in terms of standing in the club’s history.”

Kris Radlinski, the Wigan chief executive, said: “Today we mourn one of our greatest ever Warriors and rugby league’s first knight. Time moves on, as it must, but some names endure. Billy Boston will always be one of them. His place in the history of Wigan, and in the history of rugby league, is secure for ever.

“I visited him on Sunday ­morning with Mandy [Johnston, Wigan’s administrator], held his hand and told him we loved him. Rest in peace, Billy. My friend, our Warrior and a true Wigan legend.”

Eamonn McManus, the chair of Wigan’s biggest rivals, St Helens, described Boston as a “giant amongst giants”, said: “Sir Billy Boston was more than an all-time great of the sport of rugby league. His name both symbolised and transcended it. He was one of the greats for both Wigan and Great Britain in the golden era of our sport in the 1950s and 60s. He was a giant amongst giants.

“He led and epitomised our sport’s and our communities’ ­pioneering example in breaking down racial ­barriers in this country and he should be remembered always for that. Although deeply saddened by his passing we should in equal measure celebrate his unparalleled contribution to our sport and to our society.”

Badenoch plotted to remove Sunak as PM months before election, book claims

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 15:05:00 GMT

Anthony Seldon’s book alleges Badenoch asked fellow Tory ministers ‘if anyone was interested in changing the captain’

Kemi Badenoch plotted with fellow Conservative cabinet ministers to remove Rishi Sunak as prime minister months before the general election, it has been claimed.

Anthony Seldon, who has written political biographies of every prime minister since John Major, has alleged in a new book that Badenoch, who was business secretary at the time, phoned several other cabinet ministers to ask “if anyone was interested in changing the captain”.

An ally of Badenoch, who is now the Conservative leader, described the claim as “total bollocks”.

The book about Sunak’s time as prime minister, which is being serialised in the Independent, says Badenoch did not respect Sunak, who she believed had been rude to her. Citing a series of sources, it says she sought to oust Sunak in 2023, when he faced considerable internal pressure over migration policy.

It quotes one Conservative MP, who the book says is now a member of Badenoch’s frontbench team, as saying she was “a menace who orchestrated trouble in the cabinet” under Sunak.

The book, titled Sunak at 10: The Last Conservative PM?, cites another unnamed “insider” as saying Badenoch “was actively looking at bringing Sunak down, constructing imaginary cabinets and offering jobs”.

After Robert Jenrick resigned as immigration minister in December 2023 over the details of Sunak’s plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, the book says Badenoch discussed telling Sunak she would resign from the cabinet if he did not amend the policy, with some people recounting that Badenoch “had promised she would ‘take him out’”.

It was at this point, the book says, that Badenoch contacted other cabinet ministers to see if any wanted a change in PM. It says she wanted “to avoid the image of wielding the knife”.

Danny Kruger, a then Conservative MP who, like Jenrick, has since defected to Reform, told Seldon that Badenoch “definitely wanted” to remove Sunak and replace him “but was concerned about being a fag-end prime minister” given the looming election.

Seldon says in the book that Badenoch decided against any challenge because she thought this would lead to her being blamed for an election defeat. It also says another reason for caution was Badenoch’s worry that she might lose a leadership contest to Penny Mordaunt, the then leader of the Commons.

The book says the plotting prompted Sunak to condemn what he called “attention-seeking” rebels and he told allies: “They probably want me to tell them to fuck off so they can pontificate, but I have a country to run. I’m not going to rise to the bait.”

Sunak said the impression of plotting and infighting pushed down the Tory vote and made the eventual election defeat in July 2024 even worse.

Badenoch was in the cabinet throughout Sunak’s time as PM, first as trade secretary and then business secretary. She had stood to become Conservative leader in the 2022 internal party contest after Boris Johnson announced he was stepping down, finishing fourth behind Liz Truss, Sunak and Mordaunt. Sunak became prime minister without a contest after Truss’s premiership imploded in just 45 days.

After the general election defeat, Badenoch became Tory leader, beating Jenrick in a vote of Conservative members.

Dissatisfaction with Sunak was far from uncommon among Conservative MPs and ministers as the party headed towards what was seen as an inevitable election defeat, even if most accepted he had inherited a near-impossible situation.

There was little appetite for yet another change of leader, however, which would have brought about a sixth Conservative prime minister inside eight years.

Sunak’s office was contacted for comment.

The Airport Chaplain review – thoroughly bingeable TV about ‘Batman in a hi-vis vest’

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 15:00:18 GMT

This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-go

Hugo Weaving plays the eponymous airport chaplain in this pacy and moreish eight-part series, which was co-created by Elise McCredie and Jude Troy, and directed with jittery flair by Bonnie Moir and Tig Terera. In case you were wondering, yes, that profession really does exist.

I doubt the lives of real airport chaplains are anywhere near as frenetic as those of this show’s protagonist, Tobias Wallace (Weaving), whose existence is a testament to that old saying: “Not all heroes wear capes.” Sometimes, they wear hi-vis.

The Airport Chaplain wastes no time establishing Tobias as a gallant do-gooder determined to save the day, as he rescues the toy rabbit of a distressed child. Tobias is a problem-solver, finding out-of-the-box solutions to all kinds of prickly situations, from locating lost baggage to transporting dead bodies, from intervening in cases of domestic violence to playing matchmaker, helping online lovers connect in real life. And sometimes, God forbid, he even provides spiritual counsel, such as helping a grieving son to deal with his father’s death.

But most of all, Tobias is a spectacular busybody, inserting himself into virtually every problem in the airport. This might not be entirely realistic, but it certainly makes for interesting drama. We’re thrown into the thick of it from the first episode, in which Tobias receives a call from the control room and races to the aid of a panicked boy in a hoodie just as the police arrive. It very quickly becomes clear who is really in charge here, with the cops left looking useless as Tobias takes the reins. He’s a bit like Batman in an airport.

But trouble arises when Tobias’s new boss arrives: terminal manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), who has not drunk the pastoral care Kool-Aid. During their first meeting, Mira isn’t impressed when Tobias describes his role as “primarily providing emotional, spiritual and practical support for passengers”. Nor is she thrilled when he knocks back her suggestion to file a daily work report, before abruptly leaving the meeting citing a “spiritual emergency”.

The stage is set for a good ol’ fashioned war between management and an employee who views himself as absolutely integral to the viability of the organisation he works for. And as much as viewers may instinctively side with Tobias, most of us will surely see some merit in Mira’s scepticism, which gives her increasing desire to show him the door – a solid narrative foothold.

Just as HBO’s hit medical drama The Pitt (also starring Azeez) reminds us of the power of hospitals as a central location, McCredie and Troy do something similar with airports; these are both places where virtually anybody can come through the door. In The Airport Chaplain, it is the exceptions that are the most interesting. While most people hurry from A to B, every now and then a character walks through the doors with a whole lot more going on. In the second episode, authorities – including Tobias, of course – deal with a man who has hidden Ethiopian honey in shampoo bottles. To me, this felt like a bit of a letdown; I was expecting something more sensational, like several kilograms of white powder inserted where the sun doesn’t shine.

Maybe that comes later – only the first four episodes were made available to the press – but every single one is pressure-packed, making the show thoroughly bingeable; it is perfect for Netflix (where it will launch globally, with Australia getting it on SBS and SBS on Demand).

Narratively, the structure feels a little scattered, though the writers (McCredie, Mithila Gupta, Sarah Bassiuoni and Vidya Rajan) do find a throughline that spans several episodes, in the story of a mysterious young woman, Asha Chawla (played by Kavitha Anandasivam), who is found in a prayer room, refusing to speak and without a passport or phone. Another recurring character is Cath Barnes (Claudia Karvan), a calm, pragmatic and sassy airline service manager who is good mates with the chaplain.

Tobias is, of course, the glue binding the show together. Weaving – one of the giants of Australian screen and stage – exudes a great combination of gravitas and relatability. His presence has real oomph and dynamism, but without any heightened quality that suggests you would never encounter such a person in real life. If my luggage ever disappears, I want Tobias Wallace on the case.

The Airport Chaplain is on Netflix, and SBS and SBS on Demand in Australia

Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 14:30:25 GMT

Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion

Despite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking about Abdul El-Sayed’s biceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot of fitness content in his campaign.

I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has a serious image problem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal.

“Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News website Axios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed ‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”.

Fox News would appear to reluctantly agree with the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.”

Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewole proclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.”

Sex sells too: it’s well established that voters around the world prefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016 study found that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study by the Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.)

Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960, 70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedy in the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup.

You can quibble with the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In his memoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.”

In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘I love rats but we can’t live with them’: the headache of rising rodent populations around the world

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 14:00:38 GMT

Robert Corrigan has been dealing with the ‘smart’ rodents all his life – and believes there are better solutions to deal with the growing infestation in the world’s cities

“The rodents have paid for every single bill I’ve ever had – every mortgage, every car payment, every pint of Guinness,” says Dr Robert Corrigan. “It’s been a great ride and I’m still at it.”

New York-based Corrigan is one of the most respected voices in the world of rodentology. Now in his 70s, he has devoted his entire adult life to studying rats and our relationship with them.

Last year, he and 10 other scientists published a paper describing the effect of global heating on rat populations. In 16 cities they found that rat numbers had increased dramatically, and there was a correlation between their numbers and rising temperatures.

The two most common types of rat – the black and the brown – do not hibernate, which means in places with regular winters their reproduction slows down or even stops during cold periods. Here lies the problem, says Corrigan.

“When you have repeating warm winters, one after the other, the rats benefit,” he says. For many families of rats, the warmer temperatures may only offer a marginal advantage, but the problem escalates “when you start multiplying that little bit of extra rat production by hundreds of millions of rats”.

Humans have been trying to control rats for centuries. Often an invasive species, they are vectors for disease, decimate crop yields and destabilise ecosystems as they hunt other species to extinction. At the other end of the spectrum, domesticated rats, descended from wild Norway rats, are often kept as affectionate pets.

Now, more and more scientists and public servants around the world are trying to manage rats without filling their cities with harmful poisons. Methods for doing so range from contraceptives to robust public health regulations.

The biggest issue with our current approach to rats – dumping poison on them and laying traps – is that we treat them like “any old vermin”, says Corrigan. They are in fact “smart mammals with mammal brains”.

He should know. Corrigan first got to know rats while working as an exterminator in the sewers of New York City. He worked in the sewers to save up for graduate school, where he studied rodent pest management. There he then spent weekend after weekend camping out in barns to observe rats.

“I saw things back then,” says Corrigan. “I saw kindness: that rat just brought food to another because it looked sick. I saw aggression: a bully would come around and attack other rats for no reason.”

He describes his feelings towards rats as paradoxical: “Do I love that species and do I respect it as a scientist? Heck, yes. On the other hand I know that they cannot cohabitate with us because they can kill us.”

Rats can carry pathogens that spill over into human populations. These include Weil’s disease, hantavirus or new variants of coronavirus.

And yet, of all the methods used to control rat populations, poison is not one Corrigan would recommend. “It’s a band aid,” he says.

There are compelling reasons to not throw everything at rodenticides, even though most experts – including Corrigan – do acknowledge their usefulness as a temporary corrective measure.

Firstly, as with many public health issues, prevention is better than cure. Enforcing stricter public health regulations is often more effective than letting rat populations spiral and then dumping poison on them to regain control.

Aside from the cruel, slow death they result in for rats, rodenticides are known to harm other wildlife and can end up being consumed by humans – in the US there are already thousands of accidental human rodenticide poisonings each year.

One hope for better managing rat populations are fertility controls, which are increasingly popular in the US following public concern about wildlife poisoning from rodenticides. Europe is slowly catching up as more experts champion the technology, which uses contraceptives to slow down rat population growth.

“Developing new forms of birth control is the key to managing the soaring number of poison-resistant rats compassionately,” said Richard Parr, director of UK charity the Center for Wild Animal Welfare. At the same time, he says outdated biocidal product regulation in the EU is “stifling innovation”. While the EU’s regulation is under review, it is not yet equipped to deal with new fertility control technology, creating uncertainty that deters investment.

But Steven Belmain, professor of ecology at the University of Greenwich, maintains a scepticism about the idea that fertility controls are advanced enough to help.

“People are sometimes quite naive thinking we can use fertility control. If you’ve got a rat in your house, you’re not going to feed it contraceptives and just let it live there with you,” he says.

“Our restaurants, our hotels, our hospitals, our food warehouses will all just collapse without having any sort of poison management.”

Back in New York, Corrigan is trying to find more evidence that fertility controls are a viable alternative to poisons, but ultimately believes infestations come from a failure of municipal politics. If one person has poor sanitation habits, it will cause an infestation that affects all.

“Cities are not strict enough on punishing people that ruin the block or the area or the province for everybody,” he says.

But one significantly populated area stands out globally as one of the only places that has managed to almost entirely eradicate rats.

Canada’s oil-rich western province of Alberta is the only place on Earth with a significant number of people, but a negligible rat population. At the centre of their success is collective effort, not fruitless chemical warfare.

Karen Wickerson is the Alberta government’s rat and pest specialist. She runs a programme that has been operational since 1950 and is one of the most successful examples of invasive species management of the last century.

After the second world war, Alberta was the breadbasket of Canada, which in turn was providing the allied forces with much-needed grain. So when rats were discovered on their eastern border with Saskatchewan, the provincial government took decisive action.

“There was a rat patrol that went out and started eradicating all the infestations along the border. At that time there were probably six or seven hundred infestations a year,” says Wickerson. In 2025, Alberta had just five infestations across the province. While the local government does use anti-coagulants and traps to kill rats, the scale of the issue is almost non-existent thanks to a proactive population.

From the very beginning, the Albertan government mobilised every citizen against rats: legislation was passed requiring them to control or report rodents on their property. At the same time a public education programme was launched: pamphlets were handed out, posters put up, and taxidermied specimens were placed in all the agriculture offices on the border.

Wickerson has one of the posters from 1990 behind her on the wall. It shows a rat with glowing red pupils in the shape of the province, staring down menacingly at its onlooker.

But even Albertans are nervous about the future of rat control. In 2026, people are taking more holidays outside of the province, bringing back rodent hitchhikers on their return. Even more significant is the development of urban areas, which creates more sanitation issues that can lead to infestation. Finally, Wickerson points out that last autumn was extremely warm, which undermines the natural protections they have as a cold province with tough winters.

Hundreds of people around the world are trying to figure out a way to address increasing rat populations, and few are in doubt about the impact the climate crisis is having. Corrigan puts it simply: “Planet Earth is changing and the rats are benefiting.”

US Catholic churches see a record number of conversions: ‘It’s a real shift’

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 14:00:38 GMT

After decades of declining religious affiliation, churches in southern California have seen an increase among gen Z

Alicia Martinez pulls on an oversized, chocolate-brown leather jacket – an incongruous choice for the July heat in Los Angeles. Later that day, she plans to see The Odyssey in a frigid theater. But first, there is mass.

Martinez, 24, enters Our Savior Parish, the castle-like church beside her workplace, the University of Southern California. Inside, she dips her fingers in holy water, makes the sign of the cross on her forehead, and enters the main part of the church in hushed reverence.

Seated in the pews, backed by the dancing light of stained-glass windows, she’s flanked by faith of all ages. Some wear chapel veils. Others sport USC-branded apparel. All huddle shoulder-to-shoulder. At summer’s peak at USC, a secular university synonymous with Hollywood and Trojan football, another institution is quietly gaining ground: the Catholic church.

More than a year ago, the Catholic faith called to her like “a pounding noise in her heart”, Martinez said, even though she has Protestant roots. This year, she completed the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults program (OCIA), the Catholic church’s formal initiation process for adults.

The parish growth mirrors a larger trend. In April, when the Catholic church traditionally registers new members, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles reported 8,598 people preparing to be baptized or formally entering the church – the highest number of reported initiations for an archdiocese in the US, and a 54% increase from 2025. Across the US, the number of adults entering the Catholic church has climbed each year since the pandemic-low, according to a survey of dioceses.

The increases have prompted talk of a religious revival. But experts say it’s too early to call it a trend. Religious disaffiliation and conversion are always in flux, says Michele Dillon, a sociology professor and dean of the College of Liberal Arts at the University of New Hampshire. Still, it’s an interesting moment for the church in the US, after decades of declining religious affiliation.

Our Savior baptized 16 people this year, a record high, said Father Matt Wheeler, the pastor. Sixty-nine people enrolled in its OCIA program, a 57% increase from last year. Mass attendance grew so significantly that church leaders have, on occasion, redirected worshippers to an overflow area to watch a live stream.

During mass, Wheeler often looks out at the sea of student faces and marvels to himself, “Wow. Nobody dragged these young adults here.”

Martinez said that for her, the call of Catholicism was amplified by the loneliness of living in a big city, where she felt battles of good and evil were constantly unfolding before her eyes.

“There’s so much wrong in the world,” said Martinez. She was drawn to Matthew’s Gospel, she said, which warns that as lawlessness increases, people’s love for one another will grow cold.

For 20-year-old Kathryn Glavin, too, global crises – including war, injustice and division – lent urgency to the search for steadier ground in faith. For most of her life, she considered herself agnostic. Then, two years ago, the UC Santa Barbara student began noticing the Catholic church’s charitable work in her community. “I feel like it’s a dark time for a lot of people in the world,” said Glavin. “And I think that naturally is going to get people who reach for the light.” In April, Glavin was baptized at St. Mark’s University Parish in Isla Vista, a student enclave cradled by UC Santa Barbara and the Pacific Ocean.

At St Mark’s, interest in Catholicism is blossoming, said Father Ryan Thornton. Established in 1965 to serve UC Santa Barbara, a secular university, the church is located between three fraternity houses – right in the middle of student life. At first, the parish understood the growing interest in Catholicism as part of a Covid-era holdover when church gatherings were temporarily restricted. But six years later, the parish has seen its largest initiation class – 56 people, said Thornton.

“That clearly can’t be about the pandemic because the difference is too far,” said Thornton. “So, then the question is, ‘Well, what’s happening now?’”

Once popular reasons to join the Catholic church, such as family pressure or a plan to marry a Catholic partner, have largely fallen away. Today, becoming Catholic is an active choice, said Thornton.

He and other church leaders suspect the new generations of faithful, many raised by non-religious parents, have emerged spiritually hungry from a steady diet of social media reels and Love Island watch parties. Catholicism offers a counterweight: rituals and a history that reaches far beyond the algorithm.

“In some ways, the superficiality of our society – the Instagrammable life – has been tried and found wanting,” said Thornton.

The increase in initiations in Los Angeles and Santa Barbara is set against a backdrop of a decades-long national shift away from organized religion. For decades, Catholicism in the US has lost more people than it has gained through religious switching – people who move to another religious tradition or no religion – according to Pew Research Center studies. But the “nones” – people who identify as atheist, agnostic, or “nothing in particular” – have leveled off in recent years, according to another Pew Research study.

Even if the increase in new Catholics reflects a new national shift, one strong year cannot reverse decades of gradual decline, said Maureen Day, a sociologist and theologian. Still, Day said, the local data could signal that religion is appealing to people in new ways – and the losses could begin to reverse.

What could signal a true reversal is sustained participation in church life, said Day. But that is difficult to track, especially at university parishes, where students graduate and move away. No one calls their former pastor to report that they are still going to church, Thornton said.

Publicly available data do not show which parishes drove the archdiocese-wide increase. But Dillon said parishes’ increases shouldn’t be dismissed.

“It’s real,” said Dillon. “It’s a real observable shift in those individual parishes and dioceses.”

Catholicism, with its centuries of tradition, elaborate rituals and thicket of rules, can intimidate newcomers. But parish leaders said it’s helped that participants these days have more accessible entry points. They listen to Father Mike Schmitz’s podcasts. They can pray in the car with their Hallow app. And they can watch Bishop Robert Barron’s YouTube channel. Our Savior Parish leaders are intentional about making the gospel relatable to a younger audience, said Wheeler. At a July mass, he referred the congregation to his latest Instagram reel.

John Ceballos said that what’s made a difference for him is the gentler message at Our Savior Parish. Ceballos was baptized Catholic, but he stopped practicing in his 20s, in part, because of the fire-and-brimstone messaging.

“It was like, ‘Oh, here we go. You know, we’re all going to hell,’” says Ceballos with a laugh. Now, at Our Savior Parish, he says mass is all about love and community. “Now, everybody’s good. Everybody’s a child of God.”

This year, Ceballos, 50, was the oldest participant in Our Savior’s OCIA program. The age gap became a running joke: Do you even know what a fax machine is? But when they began studying Catholic teachings, the age gap fell away: everyone was a beginner.

Near the end of mass at Our Savior Parish, Catholics come forward in a communion procession to receive what the church teaches is the body and blood of Christ. Even in the summer, when many USC students are away, the procession threads along the entire length of the church. As it stretches on, people kneeling in prayer shift on their knees. Others sit.

Aidan Freire has attended mass at Our Savior Parish for two years. Although another parish is less than a mile away, he is drawn to this one because of its energy.

“I feel like this parish is really good because everyone’s young,” said Freire, 19.

To him, the clearest measure of the parish’s draw comes during Communion, which is reminiscent of another experience.

“It’s like a TSA security line.”

At least one in four former NFL players in study suffered from degenerative brain disease CTE

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 13:44:16 GMT

215 of 235 donated brains showed signs of CTE

Condition can only be diagnosed after death

Symptoms include problems with memory and mood

At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic ⁠traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a study released on Tuesday.

Out of the 878 former players who died during that time frame, 235 donated their brains for study, researchers said, with 215 ⁠of those donated brains ⁠found to have CTE, ​a degenerative disease that can only definitively be diagnosed after death. CTE is associated with repeated blows to the head, including concussions. Symptoms include difficulty with attention and memory, dementia, mood disorders and headaches.

An NFL spokesperson said: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.

“The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust – and expanding – set of resources to enhance their physical and ⁠mental well being.

“We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about ​their health.“

The study’s lead author Daniel Daneshvar, the chair ‌of physical medicine and rehabilitation ‌at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries are ‌a known factor in elevated rates of neurodegenerative disease.

“Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population,” he added.

The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion + CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels ‌of the sport.

“The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn’t occur at the NFL level. They occurred at the collegiate level … and at the high school ​level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk,” Daneshvar said.

A number of high-profile NFL players who took their own lives – including Junior Seau, Dave Duerson and Aaron Hernandez – were found to have had CTE when their brains were analyzed after their deaths.

The NFL’s 2011 collective bargaining agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.

The US supreme court cleared the way for the NFL’s settlement of ⁠concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.

“If the changes that have been ​implemented at the NFL level, including reducing ​the amount of contact in sports practices ​to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth ​levels, athletes would be ‌better off,” said Daneshvar, ​who urged current and former ​athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative disease expert evaluation.

“We know that nearly 70% of head impacts are occurring in practice. So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives.”

Three years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you?

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 13:35:23 GMT

The crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too?

How reassuring to learn that police investigating claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed have handed a file to the Crown Prosecution Service, a mere three years after the former Harrods owner’s death at the age of 94, and just decades after the first survivors made reports of abuse. The CPS has said it won’t provide a timescale for any decision, to which we might remark: no shit. With this case, the one thing you could never accuse any of the authorities of is being bound by anything approaching a timescale.

The story does, however, certainly have scale. So far, more than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Al Fayed by at least 156 women – abuse he got away with, having died without any charges ever being brought against him. The claims span the years 1977 to 2014. At least 21 women came forward while he was alive, and there have been extraordinary rundowns in news articles and documentaries about all the alleged enablers of his wicked behaviour, from lawyers to mouthpieces to security henchmen to the doctors who carried out “purity examinations” on his young female PAs.

So, not to be a Debbie Downer – because any movement on this case is better than none – but perhaps that sense of scale is not immediately discernible from the file that has been sent to the CPS, which relates to a male suspect in his 80s and two indecent assaults on two women in London. The investigation remains ongoing, the Met confirms.

Of course, other under-prosecuted criminal networks are available. During the full-spectrum coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein case, many asked how on earth so many blind eyes could be turned by so many people to so much flagrant abuse by someone who was known to have served prison time for soliciting prostitution from a minor. People marvelled at the vast collective silence – yet anyone who couldn’t quite believe how it could happen should have been reassured that other vast collective silences were very much ongoing. Peter Mandelson’s now notorious message of commiseration to his friend Jeffrey shortly before his 2008 incarceration – “it just could not happen in Britain” – always seems to me ironically resonant. Perhaps his lordship was right, though not in the way he meant.

As the Epstein furore raged on earlier this year, several Al Fayed survivors wrote to me asking why this one case was dominating everything while another, still unresolved one – and so much closer to home – seemed to lack the turbocharge of outrage that pushes something from the places our society would rather forget into the ones where we have our (always belated) reckonings. The answer to that question is normally that significant numbers of people and institutions have a deeply vested interest in not getting to the bottom of it.

It would feel unwise to conclude anything other than that in this case. There has been no equivalent political pressure to let daylight in on Al Fayed’s activities. No one has got wall-to-wall news coverage for asking how he was able to operate an alleged criminal fiefdom in the centre of Knightsbridge, when allegations were repeatedly made and the rumours in rarefied circles were more than deafening. It was, it seems, just the way things were.

And as indicated, for things to be that way for so long, there needed to be whole armies of enablers and hangers-on who facilitated abuse, or looked away, or closed down or ridiculed or trashed those who stepped out of line and said anything about it, including the alleged victims. Only one of Epstein’s helpers, Ghislaine Maxwell, has ever been brought to justice. Typically, no one bar the kingpin in what I think of as the sex-case industrial complex even faces so much as a charge – they simply melt back into society, into other jobs, into the ongoing conspiracy of silence.

Today, the Al Fayed survivors’ group Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors issued a statement pointing out that: “Survivors have spent decades either not being believed or being told that Fayed and those around him were too powerful and that nothing could be done – but today is an important reminder that the passage of time does not, by itself, put accountability beyond reach.” Yet with the best will in the world, the passage of time doesn’t exactly help, does it? Al Fayed himself died unscathed, and we all know that once things tip conveniently into the “historical” file, they are so much harder to prove.

But there are things the public can get behind right now. What Al Fayed’s survivors want is the trafficking investigation they have been requesting for almost two years. As they point out, this was not one bad man, nor some form of corporate abuse. It was, they allege, a trafficking network involving multiple perpetrators and enablers and backed by the global movement of illicit funds. At least five survivors have already been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of modern slavery. Yet the Met has been accused of having failed in its legal duty to offer the victims a referral to the national referral mechanism (it’s understood the police didn’t believe they were obligated to), which identifies modern slavery victims. Yet again, all the running is being made by a survivors’ group. No One Above wants confirmation that human trafficking and modern slavery are the primary framework of the Al Fayed investigation, and to know that financial investigators are being utilised to determine how the network was funded and concealed.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It remains to be seen if any belated percentage of justice will be served in this case. Even if it is, we can expect all manner of blind-eye institutions to immediately resort to their happy place and trot out some trite platitude like “never again”. In fact, it would be more accurate to conclude the opposite. Always again. Always again, until society has the courage to realise that it so often takes a village to do bad things, as well as good ones.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

‘An enchanting oasis’: Venetian island with Napoleonic fort up for sale

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 13:21:18 GMT

Smaller than a football pitch, Crevan has a rich history – but how rich its buyer needs to be is strictly under wraps

An island in the Venice lagoon boasting a Napoleonic fort and lush gardens is up for sale.

Described as an “enchanting oasis of peace and beauty”, Crevan offers a “spectacular view” of Venice’s main island, but is far from its crowds.

Located a few minutes by boat from the islands of Burano and Torcello and just slightly smaller than the size of a standard football pitch, Crevan was built in 1806 by the French military during the Napoleonic era as a strategic outpost to defend the northern Venetian lagoon from the Austrian empire.

But in 1815 the island fell under Austrian rule before passing to the Italian state in 1866, after the annexation of Veneto to the Kingdom of Italy. Crevan continued to serve a military purpose until after the first world war.

After years of neglect, it was bought by a private owner and its buildings restored as residential properties.

Its most prominent feature is the Napoleonic fort, converted by the current owner into a small villa with four bedrooms and surrounded manicured lawns and vegetable and fruit gardens and trees. There is also a private mooring along the island’s small internal canal, and a helipad.

Crevan has been listed for sale by several top property agencies, including Lionard Luxury Real Estate and Dimora Italian Real Estate, an affiliate of Christie’s International. The asking price, however, is strictly reserved for interested buyers.

“Crevan offers the privilege of withdrawing from the world without ever leaving the universal allure of Venice,” Dimitri Corti, the founder and chief executive of Lionard Luxury Real Estate, said in a press release. “What one acquires is not simply a residence and a piece of land, but space, privacy and an entire landscape to preserve.”

But Crevan has competition. Isola Santa Cristina, another island in the Venetian lagoon that for decades was owned by the heir to the Swarovski crystal empire, was put up for sale at about €24m in June. The luxury retreat comes with a huge villa, a saltwater swimming pool and vineyards.

An octagonal-shaped island close to the Venice lido and dating back to the 1500s, when it was built as a defence post by the Republic of Venice, is also on the market.

Five more arrested over crash that killed seven people including two police officers

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 13:20:11 GMT

A total of 17 people have now been arrested over Saturday’s crash in which car drove wrong way along dual carriageway

Five more people have been arrested by detectives investigating a crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed on Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat, which had been pursued by police, was driven the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and hit their marked armed response vehicle.

All five occupants of the pursued car – Cole Robert Worthy, 17; Theo Rae, 17; Makai Saddington, 18; Michael Robert Cahill, 23; and Jacob Matusiak, 23 – were declared dead at the scene.

Police have said the group had links to “serious and organised criminal activity” and that four of the five had a total of 37 previous convictions for offences such as possession of a bladed article, car theft, possession of drugs, racially aggravated intentional harassment, and numerous driving offences.

The crash has led to greater scrutiny on an emerging trend of young people posting videos online of cars they are in being driven dangerously. One senior figure in the Police Federation of England and Wales said young people were “baiting police officers” with reckless driving.

Paul Williams, the federation’s acting deputy national chair, told BBC Breakfast that reckless driving young people had become a “real problem” for responding officers.

“Every day we can identify now numerous examples of young people sensationalising dangerous driving. Not just dangerous driving, but baiting police officers who are out there to protect the public,” said Williams.

He added: “It’s a real problem. It’s causing officers concern. They shouldn’t have to be going out and worrying about whether they’re going to return home from their shift or not. But on top of that, wondering if they’re going to be plastered all over social media. It’s absolutely unacceptable and social media platforms need to take some action.”

The five arrests on Tuesday came a day after Cleveland police announced 12 people, nine men and three women, had been arrested after officers said they received several reports of two vehicles, the VW Passat and a Volvo XC60, being driving dangerously at the time.

Of those 12, four were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and four on suspicion of possessing a firearm, while four of the suspects were also accused of possessing class A and B drugs with intent to supply.

Two of the 12 people previously arrested have now appeared in court. Kai Beattie, 19, appeared at Teesside magistrates court charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life. Cameron George, 26, was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside crown court on 21 September charged with drugs offences and possession of criminal property.

The five arrested on Tuesday were a boy aged 16, an 18-year-old and a man of 21, all on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group; a 55-year-old on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old on suspicion of making threats to kill.

Road safety statistics up to 2025 also show a trend in dangerous driving for young people, particularly young men, being on the rise, with 77 people aged between 16 and 20 dying last year, compared with 65 the year before and 55 in 2016, the largest rise of any age group.

The government has acknowledged the need to challenge social media companies that platform videos which encourage dangerous driving among people, with a Downing Street spokesperson saying on Monday that No 10 would give the regulator Ofcom its “full backing to take tough action” on any sites and apps that do not moderate or remove such content.

The crash in Middlesbrough is one of several incidents involving people being killed or hospitalised due to a car trying to evade police that have occurred in the past fortnight across the UK, with a similar accident taking place in England on Tuesday, when a crash after a police pursuit in Warwickshire led to a man dying and a woman being hospitalised.

In Ireland last week, another similar incident resulted in four people, including a seven-year-old boy, being hospitalised when a car containing five teenagers drove into them on the M9 in County Kildare to evade Garda. All five teenagers were killed.

A fundraiser set up by Cleveland police federation for Blades’ and Clough’s families has exceeded £750,000 in donations.

We asked our climate reporters to highlight one idea for positive change. We got a chronicle of global transformation

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 12:27:21 GMT

There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope

Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support

The news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and the world.

But as news stories typically need to be about new developments or things people didn’t previously know about, it can be hard to cover all those brilliant initiatives being undertaken in the background – no matter how cheering they are. Which is why, back in 2023, we decided to ignore the usual rules about what constitutes “news” and start writing about them anyway. Readers, we knew, would like to hear about them.

And so was born the Alternatives, a weekly news column where we cover these different projects. We’re constantly amazed by some of the things we learn. Norway has heat pumps in two-thirds of its homes. China’s sponge cities are targeting 70% rainwater reuse. Paris is building a gigantic cooling machine using river water. It feels as if the series is a vast chronicle of the transformations that are taking place everywhere, far faster than we sometimes realise.

This year, as part of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign, we are highlighting all of the work that our environment team does to bring readers positive ideas such as those above, providing hope that a better world is possible if we start acting on it.

So, we asked our environment reporters around the world to share one big idea from their journalism – funded by you – that has helped drive or inspire some kind of positive change for the planet. Their answers are below.

Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of support

Climate and environment reporter, Guardian Australia

Many objections to wind turbines cite the impact on wildlife, such as birds and bats. But there are simple fixes and innovations that demonstrate there doesn’t need to be a trade-off between clean energy and safeguarding biodiversity. One such approach I reported – which involves raising the “cut in” speed at which turbines start spinning – has the potential to save tens of thousands of native bats every year, with minimal impact on energy output.

European environment correspondent

Sausage-hungry and schnitzel-loving Germany is not a likely place for plant-based food to boom, but it’s a case study in how individual green choices have a surprisingly powerful ripple effect. I reported on the hospitals winning patients over as they change menus to enable healthier diets with more plants and less meat.

Environment editor

When everything seems wrapped in gloom, we need fresh thinking and some can-do attitude. That’s why I loved interviewing Mariana Mazzucato, one of the world’s leading economic and social thinkers, about her stimulating ideas of re-basing politics on the global common good. She shows that we can change the world for the better, including fixing the climate crisis, and though she advises global leaders , she also believes the joy we can bring to our daily lives – like carnivals and communal eating – can be just as powerful.

Environment editor

When I reported in 2020 that microplastic pollution had been discovered at the top of Mount Everest, it showed that humanity’s litter had polluted the entire planet. But it also inspired a young researcher to set up an award-winning project that is now recycling plastic in Nepal into much-needed insulation for homes and stopping the waste contaminating the high mountain nation.

Global environment writerI covered a new report by Thomas Piketty and co at the World Inequality Lab, which shows us that a just and equitable world is possible. I also highlighted how new energy is bringing a new world order, with China dominating the energy transition with astonishing results, while fossil fuel fascists in the US try to turn back the clock.

Senior climate reporter, Guardian US

A barley farm in the US Pacific Northwest had been quietly leeching pollutants into the nearby watershed. It has long been an issue along the southern Oregon coast, where 95% of the sprawling networks of wetlands were drained, diverted, or dried, and replaced by cattle ranges and crops. But when Karl Wenner acquired the land in 2021, he wanted to try something new. By restoring a wetland on just 28 of the farm’s 162 hectares, he created a welcome sanctuary for migrating and native birds that are disappearing from the area, endangered native fish who can be spotted swimming near rows of sprouting barley, and the plants that quickly soaked up the phosphorus, stopping run-off. The remarkable transformation was not only beneficial to the environment – it was a boon to business. The story showcased a symbiotic solution to one of the world’s most pressing environmental problems.

Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:04:56 GMT

Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running

The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.

Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.

Analysis by the non-profit group Foxglove reveals that when fully operational, the Wapseys Wood datacentre in Buckinghamshire and the Quest Park datacentre in Bedfordshire will use 1.3GW of power and will produce more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions.

ExxonMobil emitted 3.9m tonnes in 2023, according to the global energy thinktank Ember.

AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are currently 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.

Because of the long wait to connect to the grid, the Wapseys Wood and Quest Park datacentres are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations.

Based on government figures on the carbon intensity of electricity generation, Foxglove has calculated these projects will produce 4.577m tonnes of carbon emissions per year.

A government spokesperson said these figures were “misleading” because of the assumption that both projects will run at 100% utilisation from day one, which they said was “not accurate”.

Tom Hegarty, head of communications at Foxglove, said assuming a 100% utilisation rate followed standard industry practice.

Kierra Box, a trade and environmental regulation campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said the aim was for datacentres to increase load and run at full capacity, and so it was “valid to look at those top level predictions”.

The former England and Wales Green party leader Caroline Lucas described the projected emissions from these projects as “absolutely horrifying”, and said it should be ringing alarm bells right across government.

The government says its own analysis shows there are multiple pathways for this rapid datacentre rollout to fit within the seventh carbon budget, which sets out how the government will reach its international climate targets.

However there remains a high level of uncertainty over how this will work.

Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, which is leading an inquiry into the environmental impact of datacentres, said this analysis was a “potent reminder that without the right measures in place, data centres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals”.

Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said the two projects were “catastrophic for our carbon budgets”. He said the only way the rapid rollout of datacentres could fit within these budgets was if other elements of the economy were given much stricter carbon budgets.

Sam Hunter-Jones, a ClientEarth lawyer, said every megawatt powering a datacentre connected to the grid was a megawatt that could not be used to replace fossil fuels elsewhere. “The reality is that unchecked datacentre growth is making the transition away from fossil fuels harder, not easier,” he said.

The datacentres are two of the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP) regime. This regime allows developers to rapidly deliver infrastructure projects by bypassing local planning authorities with decisions instead handled by central government.

Hayes said it was a “very worrying sign” that the government had allowed two gas-fired datacentres to apply into the NSIP regime. “I think that sends an extremely bad signal and demonstrates that they are not serious about addressing the emissions associated with datacentres,” he said, describing it as an “affront to local people”.

Lucas also raised concerns about the projects being fast-tracked, and said it “insulates” them from local scrutiny.

“In order to be able to make sensible decisions on which projects should go ahead and where they should be, we need to have more information in the public domain. We need to have more scrutiny, not less, and yet things like the NSIP regime are moving things in the opposite direction,” she said.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Datacentres are a vital part of our economy and our everyday lives, helping us interact with the services we need, while driving growth and renewal for communities. We will enable the development and growth of new industries, such as datacentres, by building unprecedented amounts of clean power.”

Wapseys Wood declined to comment. Quest Park did not respond to a request for comment.

‘The day I disclose, my career is over’: the journalist facing an $800 daily fine to keep her sources secret

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:00:35 GMT

If Catherine Herridge’s petition to the US supreme court fails, she’ll be on the hook for a daily fine until she discloses her sources – a case unsettling press freedom organizations

For 18 days this summer, veteran journalist Catherine Herridge walked to her Washington DC mailbox and dropped off a check for $800. The money was required by law to cover a judge-imposed sanction after she was found in contempt of court in 2024 for refusing to disclose her sources. It fell to her 21-year-old son James to provide the moral support Herridge needed. “He understands the pressure that I’ve been under,” she said. “It was very hard, personally.”

The check drop is now on hold. The judge who issued that order, Christopher R Cooper, has since clarified that Herridge doesn’t need to pay the fine until she has a chance to plead her case to the supreme court, which she petitioned late last week.

If that petition is unsuccessful, and there is good reason to believe it will fail, then something rather extraordinary in American history will commence: Herridge will be on the hook for the daily fines until or unless she reveals her sourcing for a series of 2017 stories about the Chinese-American scientist Yanping Chen, who had been federally investigated – but not charged – over her ties to China’s military and whether a Virginia school she operated was secretly aiding the communist country.

It’s a case that has unsettled not only Herridge and her family, but also the community of press freedom organizations that exist to ensure against the unthinkable – a reporter being forced to disclose confidential sources, shattering the foundation of national security reporting in the public interest.

“Reporter-source confidentiality is the lifeblood of investigative journalism,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation. “Whistleblowers in a position to expose abuses won’t trust journalists to protect them, and won’t come forward, if they believe reporters will be threatened with financial ruin for not outing them in court.”

Unless the supreme court intervenes, or the matter is resolved via a settlement, that worst case scenario might be just around the corner.

“I built my career on developing confidential sources, and the day I disclose, my career is over,” Herridge, 62, said in an interview last week in a law firm conference room a few blocks from the White House. “I mean, I’m finished. How can anyone trust me in the future? But it’s bigger than me. I’m in the last chapter of my career. This is really for people who have another 10 or 20 years ahead of them, and for another generation of journalists. It’s for their benefit.”

Still, she acknowledged, “the fines are designed to break you as a journalist, mentally and financially.”

Although Herridge was found in civil contempt, if she refuses to pay the daily fine, she could be held in criminal contempt and put in jail.

Herridge has only been able to pay the fees and litigate the case with the support of her former employer, Fox News, which has continued to cover her top-level legal representation even though she has not worked for the network in seven years.

“This is a landmark first amendment case – probably one of the most important first amendment cases in two decades,” Herridge said. “And I have made a decision, with the backing of Fox, that I’m going to defend these principles.”

She praised the network’s support, saying: “Fox News is doing something that other media organizations have not done: they are going to the mat for their reporter. They are going to the mat for the free press and the first amendment in an environment where other media outlets have settled. And I would not be where I am today unless they were paying my legal fees. This is something that would be crippling for any journalist.”

In a statement, a Fox News spokesperson said: “Forcing journalists to unmask their sources under threat of government coercion sets a dangerous precedent that will chill investigative journalism and prevent future whistleblowers from holding the powerful accountable. We have remained steadfast in our support of Catherine Herridge in this gravely important battle to preserve press freedoms and will continue to fight this egregious assault on the first amendment.”

There are no shortages of lawsuits involving journalists these days, with Donald Trump a frequent filer of specious billion-dollar claims over reporting he doesn’t like.

Herridge’s case is unique in part because she was not actually the target of the original lawsuit, which does not contest the accuracy of her reporting. Chen filed the case in 2018 under the Privacy Act, suing four government agencies – the FBI, the Department of Justice, the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security – over what she said was the government’s “illegal and unwarranted public disclosure of her personal information” to a journalist (Herridge).

After deposing numerous government officials, Chen’s team remained unable to find the source who provided the information – and lobbied a judge to force Herridge to cough up her source or sources. The judge, agreeing with Chen that Herridge was her only remaining avenue for providing the information she needed to litigate the case, ordered the journalist to reveal the information, something she has repeatedly refused to do.

But Herridge, who is just a witness in the case, said she “doesn’t think it’s the role of a journalist to provide evidence against the government”.

Press freedom advocates have seconded that argument.

“Allowing civil litigants to commandeer journalists to help them prove their cases is arguably even more harmful than letting the government do so,” Stern said.

But Chen’s team – led by attorney Andrew Phillips – has argued that her rights as a citizen should supersede any special privilege provided to a journalist, an argument that has been well received by the US court of appeals for the DC circuit.

“Dr. Chen, like any other American citizen, is entitled to discover the identity of the federal official(s) who abused their access to an American’s private information and leaked it to cause her harm,” Phillips said in an email. “That type of unlawful conduct is exactly what the Privacy Act was designed to address. Rogue government officials who break the law and abuse their power to target private citizens should not be able to remain anonymous and free from consequences simply because they launder their unlawful conduct through a reporter.”

Chen’s case has been aided by a lack of statutory protection for reporters operating in Washington DC, which unlike many US states does not have any sort of shield law that would moot the case.

That’s why Herridge is hoping that the Supreme Court takes up the case. “If the lower court decision stands, it means that in Washington DC, where we do the bulk of the national security reporting, that journalists and sources will have the weakest protections of anywhere in the country,” she said. “For example, if I was reporting in Boston, this subpoena would’ve been thrown out years ago.”

In a filing last month, Chen’s team asked the judge to implement graduated fines that could rise to $5,000 a day – and perhaps even more significantly, to bar Herridge from being reimbursed by a third party like Fox. The judge denied that motion, meaning that for the time being, the money will not ultimately have to come out of the Herridge family’s pockets.

That is especially significant because, after being laid off by CBS News in 2024, Herridge no longer commands the network paycheck she did for decades. Instead, she is doing her own thing as an investigative journalist, without the guaranteed compensation and legal representation that comes with a full-time job.

But Herridge isn’t primarily concerned about getting back into the world of television news. She is instead focused on this case, and making sure that she can do some good for her chosen field – and the next generation of journalists – by ensuring that they won’t be forced to choose between bankrupting themselves or breaking their sacred promise to sources.

Looking back on the decades of exclusive reporting she has done for the biggest television networks in the country, Herridge says of her current court battle: “It’s the most consequential thing that I’ve done in my career.”

As a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerable

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:00:34 GMT

A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and in England and Wales, too many do not

Zubir Ahmed is a transplant surgeon and former Labour minister

As a doctor, I have spent much of my professional life caring for people at some of the most vulnerable moments they will ever face. I have seen the anxiety that surrounds the prospect of dying, and the desperate wish of patients and families to avoid unnecessary suffering.

Naturally, we all want people facing the end of life to be treated with kindness and respect. But when considering the debate on assisted dying, true compassion demands that we ask a more fundamental question. What kind of society are we building if, before we’ve fixed the systems designed to care for people, we introduce a system designed to help them die? As a former health minister who has seen the system from the inside, I am able to say it is not ready or equipped to answer this question.

Andy Burnham has been right to raise this as a priority issue at the start of his tenure as prime minister. Speaking at a care home recently, he explained that assisted dying should not be introduced while Britain’s palliative care and social care systems remain under such strain. A choice between death without adequate care and a death prematurely self-induced is not a real choice.

Indeed, as parliament prepares for yet another vote on assisted dying in England and Wales on 11 September, I fear that the offering has been somewhat mis-sold to the public. A state-controlled medicalised dying process is still a process – one where there remain risks of complication and suffering. The reality of assisted dying is more complex than the promise of a perfectly controlled death.

Many people imagine a system where a person facing a terminal illness can choose the exact moment and manner of their death, free from distress. But the legislation does not and cannot provide that certainty. A patient who self-administers medication to begin the dying process may still experience complications. The process may take time; it may require medical intervention. It may not happen where or when the person imagined. The promise of absolute control can therefore become something different in practice: an appearance of choice that does not always deliver the agency people expect.

I am far from the only medical professional to be worried about the prospect of assisted dying being available on the NHS. Among those raising concerns about the bill’s dozens of flaws have been the Royal College of Physicians, the Royal College of Psychiatrists, the Complex Life and Death Decisions (CLADD) group from King’s College London, the Royal College of Pathologists, the British Geriatrics Society and numerous other medical bodies and care authorities. The same concern comes up again and again: is it really a “free choice” when palliative care and social support fall short?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

A person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances. It can be shaped by whether they feel supported, whether they fear becoming a burden, whether their family is coping and whether they have access to the care they need. That is why the state of our care systems cannot be treated as a separate issue from assisted dying. Timely access to palliative and social care remains too often determined by where someone lives rather than what they need. For some families, excellent end-of-life support is available; for others, particularly in rural areas as well as constituencies experiencing high inequality, the experience is one of waiting, uncertainty and having to fight for services that should be guaranteed.

A Labour government founded the NHS on a principle that remains as important today as it was at its creation: that healthcare should be there when people need it most, regardless of their circumstances. A postcode lottery in care cannot be ignored while debating a new legal pathway for people at the end of their life.

In Scotland, this concern has been expressed clearly, and was an important reason why, in March, 85% of Labour MSPs voted against the legalisation of assisted dying in Holyrood. The bill introduced in Westminster by my colleague Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP for Spen Valley, in October 2024 did not fare much better: too many concerns about patient welfare meant the House of Lords would not rubber-stamp the flawed text. And yet, on 11 September, MPs will be faced with yet another vote on assisted dying before the care systems are improved to a level which even makes that debate appropriate. Andy Burnham has his priorities right: this is the wrong debate at the wrong time. This is why I, and many others, will be voting against this bill, in pursuit of comfort, dignity and appropriate care for people who are vulnerable and dying.

Zubir Ahmed MP is an NHS vascular and transplant surgeon, and served as the parliamentary under-secretary of state at the Department of Health and Social Care from 6 September 2025 to 12 May 2026.

Food has turned into a class war – and it’s ruined my appetite

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 10:00:34 GMT

More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment

Lewis Bassett is a young sociologist and chef who I first encountered through his podcast, The Full English, where he thinks about the cultural meaning of, say, Delia Smith; gazpacho; whelks. This was thinking you didn’t know you needed until you heard it. Now he’s written a book of the same name, asking: why do we eat the way we do in Britain, and why do we think the way we do, even about the stuff we wouldn’t be caught dead eating?

About 57% of all the food eaten in Britain is ultra-processed, which feels familiar from at least a decade of hand-wringing about it, but is radically defamiliarised when set against the rest of Europe. In France it’s 14%, and Italy is also in the teens. It’s amazing they don’t all live to be 150. And while this plainly has its roots in inequality, there is a hefty side order of attitude, which Bassett contemplates while working through the history of sourdough, curry and olive oil, and describing his own life cheffing in fancy kitchens and gastropubs.

Basically, we think posh food is pretentious; but what counts as “posh” constantly morphs, partly through the sheer cost of it, until even food that wasn’t posh before (like fish and chips) becomes posh, and therefore pretentious (also smaller portions: absolute sitcom signifier of despised posh food). I’m freestyling, of course, and you should read The Full English for the meat of Bassett’s argument, but it is fascinating to consider how any given ingredient is freighted with political self-fashioning.

There are so many foods – the chickpea; the Findus crispy pancake; tomatoes; the Turkey Twizzler – that have had their moment as the thing some people hate other people for eating, and it’s all shorthand for a low-level class war, mediated through food. It amps up to a thousand when parents get involved.

Bassett has this lovely, curious, unjudgmental thinking style, and concludes that “ours is a peculiar diet formed by a peculiar experience of modernity”. Still, you can’t help but think, if we could let go of some of the political and emotional charge around food, we’d end up eating things that were more delicious. I don’t mean Findus crispy pancakes – I know they’re ultra-processed. They were delicious, though.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist
