I once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches down

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 09:00:54 GMT

Nearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, the ex-NBA player is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a punchline

Nine years ago, I watched Enes Kanter ask America to take him in. It was May 2017, inside the National Basketball Players Association’s offices in midtown Manhattan. Kanter had just returned from a frightening detention at Bucharest airport, where Romanian border police told him Turkey had canceled his passport. He’d just turned 25, an NBA center with a green card and no country he could safely call home.

“I’m open for adoption,” he joked from the head of a table in a nondescript conference room, addressing a dozen reporters hastily summoned by his manager. Then he turned serious: “My next move is to just become an American citizen.”

The previous 48 hours had unfolded like a John le Carré thriller. Kanter said his manager woke him at 2.30am in Jakarta where he’d been hosting a basketball clinic because Indonesian security forces were looking for him. He hurried to Singapore, then Frankfurt, only to be stopped in Romania. He feared being sent to Turkey, where he had grown up and whose national team he had represented. There, he said, no one might hear from him again. Department of Homeland Security officials and lawyers for the Oklahoma City Thunder and the players’ union helped get him back to the United States.

Sitting in that room that Monday morning, I saw someone who had already paid a steep cost for the right to speak truth to power. Kanter called Recep Tayyip Erdoğan the “Hitler of our century”. He recounted daily death threats, a family placed in jeopardy by his opposition to Erdoğan and support for the president’s exiled rival, Fethullah Gülen, and parents he had stopped calling because he feared the government was tapping their phones. He said his father, Mehmet, a university professor, had been spat on at a supermarket. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” he told us.

The reprisals only widened. Turkey issued warrants for Kanter and later sought an Interpol Red Notice and his extradition. He skipped NBA trips abroad, including a Knicks game in London, because he feared detention or assassination. His father was dismissed, detained and charged with membership in a terrorist organization before his eventual acquittal in 2020.

In 2021, Kanter finally became an American citizen and legally added Freedom to his name. You didn’t have to squint hard to make out the symbolism. The dissident Turkey tried to render voiceless and stateless had found both an adopted home and a protected platform.

On Sunday night, I found myself thinking about the young man from that news conference – and wondering what became of him. Back then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attention.

Kanter was sitting courtside at the Chicago Sky’s game against the Indiana Fever in a shirt reading: “WOMAN noun. adult human female.” He had joined a rally outside the arena in support of Sophie Cunningham, the Fever guard who opposes transgender participation in women’s sports. In recent weeks, Kanter had also declared himself eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft, claiming to identify as a woman and posting workout videos about beginning his “transition”. (League sources have since said he is not eligible to play and dismissed his declaration as a publicity stunt the WNBA would not “give oxygen” to.)

The crudity of the attempted reductio ad absurdum was matched only by the breathlessness of the response across the Maga right, where Kanter’s stunt was greeted as an intellectual masterstroke: BRILLIANT, GOT ‘EM, CHECKMATE. Fox News has not merely covered Kanter’s bit uncritically; it has plainly participated in the mockery. Take the premise of transgender inclusion, distort it into the spectacle of a former NBA player treating womanhood as a debating prop, and wait for the audience to laugh. Yet Kanter exposed no contradiction. The punchline was simply the existence of transgender people.

No player assigned male at birth has ever competed in the WNBA. Whatever legitimate questions exist about eligibility rules, competitive balance and the place of biology in elite sport can be discussed without reducing them to a spectacle designed to humiliate those at the center of the debate. Kanter’s stunt depends on the idea that gender identity is inherently fraudulent and that trans women are simply opportunistic men waiting to invade women’s spaces. It has done nothing to clarify policy. It has merely turned a vulnerable minority into content – including many trans fans who have long regarded the 30-year-old league as one of the few places in professional sport where they belong. At a moment when ESPN’s WNBA coverage is averaging 1.4 million viewers, up 16% from the same point last season, Kanter’s stunt has hijacked a feelgood story about the league’s growth and made a phantom threat the focus instead.

The invasion rhetoric carries a bitter irony. The WNBA is not being overrun by trans women but by straight men who cannot let women have a flourishing league of their own without mocking it, manufacturing controversy and making themselves the story. Some of loudest voices posing as defenders of female athletes openly ridicule and try to humiliate them for laughs, in some cases through sexualized stunts. There is something almost pitiable about men squandering their energy and influence on belittling women whose discipline, sacrifice and extraordinary achievement have carried them to the highest level of their profession. Misogyny has simply put on the costume of concern.

In Kanter’s case, this was not simply a lone provocateur wandering into an arena. According to Talking Points Memo, the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute (AFPI) promoted Kanter’s arrival, circulated footage of his ejection and began selling a $45 “Let Freedom Play” sweatshirt featuring him in a mock-up of the WNBA logo. An AFPI executive was seated a few rows behind him, although the organization did not answer questions about whether it bought his courtside seat. Kanter, who attended the 2024 State of the Union as House speaker Mike Johnson’s guest and has said he plans to run for Congress in 2028, has political ambitions of his own.

Sign up to WNBA 30

A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.

after newsletter promotion

Whether or not there is a formal arrangement, the transaction is visible enough: Kanter lends the campaign the credibility of an 11-year NBA veteran and supplies a spectacle in which transgender people are the bait, while an organization embedded in Trump’s political network converts those assets into attention, merchandise and political capital. If it keeps voters staring at a nonexistent threat to the WNBA instead of the corruption engulfing the administration in the run-up to the November midterms, the stunt has done its real work.

Late in the third quarter of Sunday’s game, Sky guard Natasha Cloud approached Kanter, yelling and pointing in his direction. Kanter stood, spread his arms and stepped on to the court before security intervened. As he was escorted away, he stopped near the basket to argue his case, then stretched out his shirt and tried to draw a response from the crowd. He had arrived ready to provoke and left performing martyrdom.

Kanter did not suddenly discover the uses of spectacle on Sunday. In 2020, after marching with Black Lives Matter protesters in Boston, he told the Guardian that athletes should use their platforms “to spread good, and to spread the truth”. He had long understood publicity as a political tool, and with good reason: he believed international pressure helped secure his father’s acquittal. The difference is what the performance now serves.

None of this diminishes the courage Kanter showed in opposing Erdoğan. The offer of US citizenship is not a contract for ideological obedience. Human rights are not a prize withdrawn when their beneficiary later behaves immorally, nor does surviving persecution bind anyone to a prescribed worldview.

But suffering does not automatically make a person generous, either. And Kanter, more than most, should understand the mechanics of dehumanization: how a powerful movement marks a minority as dangerous, treats its identity as illegitimate and converts real human beings into totems of social decay. The scale of Erdoğan’s repression and an American culture-war stunt are not equivalent. The moral reflex behind them – identifying people with less power and making public sport of their vulnerability – should have been instantly recognizable to him. The most generous reading, perhaps charitable to a fault, is that Kanter can recognize dehumanization only when he is its target.

US citizenship gave Kanter what he asked for in that Manhattan conference room: safety, a home and the freedom to speak without Erdoğan deciding the consequences. That freedom includes the right to make a cruel spectacle of himself, but it does not exempt the spectacle from judgment.

“I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” Kanter said in 2017. I believed him. On Sunday, he used that voice to make other innocent people feel smaller. What a waste.

From Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we did

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 09:00:53 GMT

Listening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common sense

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

Every few months, there are more shocking headlines about the behaviour of England’s water companies. The latest are about the ever-increasing pay of the chief executives and chief financial officers, which rose to a total of £25.3m across 14 companies over the past year. Meanwhile, people living in England struggle with rising water bills and untreated sewage being discharged (often illegally) on to beaches and in to lakes, and companies such as Thames Water are on the brink of insolvency and want government backing.

It’s not surprising that we’re in this situation: England’s water companies have long been accused of putting the interests of shareholders above those of customers. From their perspective, the privatisation of water has been an astounding success. Between 1991 and 2019, dividends to the shareholders of the parent companies totalled £57bn, which averages out to more than £2bn every year. The majority of these private parent companies are foreign-owned, so the profits aren’t even kept in Britain.

Lack of proper oversight creates a series of perverse incentives. If water companies can charge more for the same amount of water, they’ll do that. If they can dump untreated sewage in public waterways, they’ll do that, too.

The root of the problem goes back to 1989 when Margaret Thatcher, then prime minister, privatised water in England. But right here, in the UK, there’s an example that shows that there is an alternative.

Unlike England, Scotland chose to retain public ownership of Scottish Water and, between 2002 and 2019, the company invested 35% more per household in infrastructure than the privatised English water companies. It charges users 14% less and it doesn’t pay dividends.

While Scottish Water’s CEO pay package, which adds up to more than £500k, has been criticised for being high relative to other public sector employees, it’s relatively low compared with the private pay packets south of the border. More importantly, Scottish Water is accountable to people living in Scotland, as all profit is reinvested back into water and sanitation systems, instead of going to shareholders.

I’ve lived in Scotland for over a decade and the water coming from taps is clean and delicious. Since 2018 Scottish Water’s Your Water Your Life campaign has been offering free drinking water through a network of public water stations across the country. By 2022, the water dispensed at these would have filled the equivalent of 15m plastic bottles. Water in people’s homes is paid for through local authorities charging council tax rather than customers receiving a bill from a private water-company.

As a public health expert, I’ve found it hard not to think about England’s poor water infrastructure because I can see how, across the world, and especially in low-income countries, access to this vital resource is often a matter of life or death. It took the father of epidemiology, John Snow, to identify dirty water as the cause of a large cholera outbreak in London. Clean water isn’t a luxury: it’s necessary to human health and wellbeing.

More recently, Chris Whitty, England’s chief medical officer, highlighted the worrying public health problem of sewage in England’s waterways. He reminded water companies and their directors that human faeces is making people who swim or use the water on popular beaches and rivers sick.

The normal logic of private efficiency might work in sectors of the economy where competition brings meaningful choice and innovation. Take cars: we can choose between different manufacturers, designs, fuel type and price; or even pharmaceutical companies, where competition encourages firms to develop different drugs and invest in risky research.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But what is the consumer choice in tap water? Water is water: we just need it to be clean, and hopefully to taste good and be reliably delivered through functioning infrastructure. We need the waste we flush down our toilets to be treated and made safe through sanitation systems, before being released into nature again.

Listening to the recent debates, you’d think that bringing English water companies back into public ownership was some kind of radical socialist idea. Guess what? That’s just normal life here in Edinburgh.

If water and sanitation are treated as a commodity, then companies will of course look at how much they can squeeze consumers. But water isn’t something that you can choose to go without. It’s absolutely vital to human life – you’d die without it in about three days – and should be a basic part of public infrastructure provided by government.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

From ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and me

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 08:50:04 GMT

As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom

My earliest memories of the Notting Hill carnival are of being mildly irritated. In its 1960s infancy, the event was strictly a Caribbean affair, transplanted to Ladbroke Grove as authentically as was practical. Its purpose was as obvious as its origins: giving Caribbean arrivals a chance to celebrate themselves by bringing the vibrancy of the home they left behind to these drab streets for a couple of days.

Vital as this was – and it really was – it didn’t cut much ice with surly 10- or 11-year-olds like me, being dragged around behind parading steelbands. Yes, it was great to see so many Black people out in the open together and your mums and dads laughing and having a good time, but did we need to be here? There was football to be played and bikes to be ridden, yet so many of us were being forced to walk for what seemed like miles following “old people music”.

Then as the 1970s got under way, everything changed. The London sound systems that had been establishing themselves over the previous few years – Coxsone Outernational, Jah Shaka, 6X6, Sufferah HiFi, TWJ and so on – assumed a growing presence at carnival, under the flyover or on the street. They were operated by men and women not much older than us, who understood how the post-Windrush generation defined their Blackness as they came of age in London and how, although roots and heritage were always important, we didn’t need to simply recreate the Caribbean.

The sound systems played the same choice of music we heard at dances and parties or in our own record collections, so we could find the reggae, the lovers rock, the soul and funk that soundtracked our lives right there set up outside accommodating pubs, caffs or people’s front doors. The big plus point was the sound systems were static, meaning if you weren’t dropping some foot you could stand around with your hands in your pockets, always a teenager’s default setting. Indeed the only walking you were obliged to do would be if the music wasn’t up to it or there weren’t enough people – ie women – at that particular sound, so you’d find another one. This might involve a bit of float-following, but, then again, it might not.

Refreshment was never a problem. Some Kentucky or a kebab when we were gathering at Turnpike Lane station, then load up with “supplies” before leaving, thus avoiding the so-called “carnival tax” temporarily inflating prices in Notting Hill off-licences. Our drinks of choice usually involved pre-mixing dark rum or Bacardi with Coca-Cola, or vodka with orange juice; beer was too heavy to lug around until they started selling it in those four packs held together with plastic rings. You’d drink a can, undo your belt, thread it through the empty ring and you were away. Some guys, more hardcore than me, would hang a pack off each hip then swagger round like a western gunslinger. (At this year’s Arsenal victory parade my son turned up with an insulated backpack containing rum, mixer, beer and ice that didn’t melt over the course of six hours, and I thought: “Wow! How we could have done with that at the carnival in the 70s!”)

Suddenly, the Notting Hill carnival made sense. Youngsters came down in droves because this was our carnival now, and while we appreciated what it stood for historically, we wanted to enjoy ourselves, too. You wouldn’t dream of missing it. Carnival was the place to run into familiar faces who you probably didn’t know by name and might not have seen since last year’s event but you were glad to have a quick chat with.

Just as the crowds swelled so did the area the event occupied. Sound systems would mostly set up outside the parade route, and by renting front gardens for the weekend there were smaller rigs as far as the canal up by Harrow Road to the north and Colville Terrace to the south – gentrification hadn’t been invented at that point – in between Ladbroke Grove and Chepstow Road. There were street dances of varying sizes everywhere, many doing a roaring trade selling drink or barbecue to the foolishly unprepared, and this takeover created one of the most attractive features of the weekend.

In the early 1970s, when police harassment was commonplace, racist microaggressions were a part of everyday life and the hospitality industry wasn’t living up to its name, just being able to walk about such a large area of London seeing far more people that looked like you than didn’t, enjoying a drink and a dance or just pissing about and not being bothered by anybody was simply brilliant. It was as if we owned those streets for four days. Everybody I knew went to work the following week with a bit of a spring in their step. And most likely exhausted: back in such unregulated times, revelry tended to kick off on Friday evening and go through to Monday night and Tuesday morning, with sound systems playing until the J’ouvert celebrations welcomed the sunrise.

My peak carnival years were the early 1970s through to the early 1980s; the riot of 1976 changed things. How and why it kicked off is a different conversation, but the aftermath of overpolicing, increasing regulation and media that used violence and criminality as the starting point for reporting: all of this squeezed out a degree of the joyful anarchy and spontaneity that had made it so beautiful. Many people, especially out-of-towners, became scared to go and the tens of thousands that did were aware of a palpable tension, especially around 7pm when the police moved to shut down the sound systems.

Naturally this changed the way we approached it, and perhaps the most dispiriting aspect of the shift was that an essentially self-regulating event was becoming subject to decisions being made elsewhere, giving the carnival the flavour of something being done to us rather than by us. It didn’t really matter how the content carried on evolving; the whole affair had become far too orderly. It doused the spark one bank holiday at a time, far from that untidy, magnificent era of mass-participation when anybody, just by showing up, knew they were genuinely contributing to the true essence of carnival.

But of course the Notting Hill carnival kept going. And as it reaches its 60th anniversary it seems to have been regenerating in size and spontaneity again as the next generation bring back that joyful anarchy. May the streets feel like theirs.

The war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudging

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 07:00:51 GMT

Although mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them on

‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinker Elijah’s epigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.

But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones.

These rotters are accompanied by people taking their phone or video calls out loud on speakerphone. In the early days of mobile phones it was a widely agreed social truism that the white-collar worker unselfconsciously bellowing “I’m on the train!” into their BlackBerry was a grade-A public nuisance, plausibly worthy of throwing in the stocks. Well, at least then we were only being subjected to one end of the conversation.

The spread of 5G across the country is making such unsolicited noise more possible and more common: “loudcasting”, the BBC called it in a recent in-depth look at the phenomenon. A public backlash is suddenly mounting. Never one to miss an opportunity for free press coverage, last week Wetherspoons boss Tim Martin banned it from his pubs.

It’s funny how social pressure points like this fade in and out of public view, as the technology that touches our lives evolves: 19 years ago, the same practice was christened “sodcasting” by Pascal Wyse in this newspaper – at that point there were no reels, no AI drivel, no streaming video calls, no such thing as an Instagram influencer, nor Instagram either. The moral panic back then was about tinny MP3s being played aloud from much more basic mobile phones – and the purported juvenile delinquency that had surely led to such a crisis.

I probably annoyed a lot of Guardian readers that year, writing more than 2,000 words in defence of sodcasting: more precisely, in defence of teenagers playing music on their phones on the bus, the train or otherwise in public. There was something qualitatively different about that iteration, I would argue. It was a necessary claiming of public space by people who are often bullied out of it: adults-in-training, still working out how to exist in the outside world as independent beings, still learning to navigate their own social lives, and (an underrated asset, this) learning to enjoy music together, as a group activity. For the rest of us, this form of sodcasting amounted to an occasional, brief and usually joyful burst of alfresco music – and we could all do with hearing Crazy Cousinz and Giggs more often anyway.

The 2010 furore about sodcasting followed a decade of punching down by Britain’s power-wielding adults against its most marginalised young people – the “chavs” and “hoodies” against whom New Labour and the tabloids collectively went to war, driven by the reactionary moralism of what was risibly called “the respect agenda”. A time of asbos, public spaces protection orders and curfews for young people.

Interestingly – and admittedly anecdotally; this stuff isn’t easy to measure – sodcasting 1.0 seemed to disappear as a phenomenon after a year or two. New social behaviours that emerge in response to new popular technologies tend to do so: things settle down as a new consensus on how we should all use them is slowly reached, and reached collectively.

Let’s hope that happens again, because what we are all hearing on buses and trains thanks to sodcasting 2.0 is measurably more antisocial and individualistic: for one thing, 2010’s groups of teen sodcasters weren’t changing songs every 10 seconds. For another – warning, more anecdotal analysis incoming – these days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones. It is maddening behaviour to anyone who has experienced it: like being on a bus or a train with someone who is flicking TV channels, constantly.

So, as Lenin once asked of matters of similarly grave importance: what is to be done? Last year, the Lib Dems proposed a £1,000 fine for sodcasting – an amusingly illiberal policy to make one of their centrepieces. For what it’s worth, I don’t think a fine is very useful, realistic or enforceable – though, God bless the ironclad French state, for it managed to find a way to do exactly that, fining a man €200 (£170) for taking a call on loudspeaker on a station platform.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The truth is that we have more sane and effective options for shaping public behaviour in the form of nudge messaging. Transport for London has a strong history of this, via adverts on its trains, tubes and buses. In 2008, its Considerate Travel campaign seemed to help quieten down the mobile phone DJs and its current Act Like a Friend and Travel Kind campaigns aim to address hate crime, misogynistic creeps and encourage others to help passengers who may be unwell. Sodcasting 2.0 pisses me off no end, too, but I think people can change with a little nudging.

Stefan Stern made an excellent case in these pages recently that we should all remove our headphones – and turn off the content altogether – to hear and more fully participate in the noisy, messy city around us. Hopefully we can achieve this via social consensus, gentle persuasion, and without the soundtrack of someone broadcasting AI monkey videos. And if all else fails, well, sod it: let’s nudge the culprits into the stocks.

Dan Hancox is a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities. His latest book is Multitudes: How Crowds Made the Modern World

Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 05:00:48 GMT

A fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away: this is a warning to the western alliance

The Canadians are exceedingly angry. I realise this can sometimes be difficult for foreigners to deduce, given our national struggle to express the full range of human emotion outside ice hockey riots. However, let me assure you that the prime minister Canadians saw take the stage on Saturday morning in the wake of the collapse in trade negotiations with the US was a Mark Carney practically vibrating with fury.

“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he said, in a rare press conference that was as candid and clear as he ever tends to be. “That’s fine … We’ve got the reserves, we’ve got the resilience, we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus. We’re gonna respond, we’re going to focus on what we can control and what we’re going to build.”

Canada walked out of negotiations, with a deal apparently on the verge of completion, mere hours before 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian exports were due to kick in.

Dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, scheduled to take effect on 8 September, will follow in turn. In a statement, Carney said that last-minute demands from the US were “uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” The US denied this, insisting that it was Canadians who made last-minute demands.

In subsequent interviews with Bloomberg, Canadian ambassador to the US Mark Wiseman said there was no specific item that put a deal out of reach; rather, it was a range of issues in which the text that ultimately wound up on the page – or, at least the interpretation of that text – did not align with what the Canadians thought they had agreed to. The most contentious issues appear to be related to tariffs on autos, digital and cultural policy, and the US claiming the right to veto Canada’s attempts to form trade alliances with other countries. Meanwhile, Canadians have no reason to trust this administration not to unilaterally impose new tariffs on a whim – which it has done, repeatedly, and as recently as this week.

In short, Carney noted, sometimes the US signature on trade deals is “written in pencil”.

Canadian voters, who were pensive about the prospect of any new deal with the US in the first place, have come out strongly in support of the prime minister. Despite the fact that the deal’s collapse will almost certainly entail painful economic penalties, the mood is one of sustained and general anger toward the US not born merely of trade irritants – very few Canadians have opinions about rules of origin tariffs on auto parts, or softwood lumber protections, or supply managed dairy quotas. In cordial times, these are the ordinary frictions between close friends and neighbours.

Rather, it’s an emotion born of a real and visceral sense of betrayal: that the people we trusted with shared security and military obligations, that the nation with which we allowed ourselves to grow economically interdependent, has turned on us. They are using ordinary trade irritants as an excuse to exercise mafioso-style dominance in the pursuit of our subjugation and maybe outright annexation. We know very well that this isn’t about trade.

We are being trained to know our place in the new world order that the so-called Dunroe doctrine is seeking to impose on the western hemisphere.

So how, exactly, are any of us supposed to respond when the US secretary of transportation, Sean Duffy, goes on Fox News in the aftermath of the collapse to say things like: “We provide their security for them and they take advantage of us? President Trump was the first one to go and say ‘that’s not the kind of relationship friends should have’.”

The US does not provide Canadian security – although many commentators, including myself, do criticise our lax military spending. The North American Aerospace Defense Command, or Norad, is a fully integrated entity of both the Canadian and US military. We have our own military, and our own police forces.

How are we supposed to respond, exactly, when our large and once-admired neighbour to the south repeatedly threatens to make us the “51st state”? Or when he posts gag photos of the whole of North America covered in a US flag – provocations we’re supposed to take “seriously but not literally”, as if that makes these threats less horrific or more acceptable.

What does one do when one’s closest “friend” and “ally” repeatedly threatens to disregard border treaties? Or when the US’s actual behaviour aligns perfectly with the president’s threat to use “economic force“ to push us into becoming an American state?

We don’t want to be an American state. And even if we did, we certainly wouldn’t want to be a state of whatever the US is choosing to become right now.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is not a single Canadian who wants to start a war with the US. No country in Canada’s position storms out of a trade negotiation unless it has to. No country as small and dependent on the US tells the modern imperium to get lost, and risks the consequences thereof, unless there is no other option.

What Carney – and Canada, for that matter – are trying to signal across the Atlantic is that the America we all built our expectations around is over. We cannot plan around the hope of a return to normal, even if Democrats regain power in Washington.

Canada’s location and US-integrated economy mean that we will be the first to face the reality of whatever the US becomes. And if it is coming for us, no European ally – including the UK – can expect to remain untouched, regardless of whatever “special relationship” you imagine may insulate you.

Personally, I simply cannot fathom the commentators and politicians in the UK who fail to understand this. Do you honestly imagine yourselves to be closer to the US militarily, geographically, economically, or culturally than Canada? Guys, we are a little America, albeit with a steadier political system and the king on the money. If they are willing to vassalise us, what sentiment of history or tradition remains to protect you?

A fundamental break in American values and objectives is not a problem that can be contained. It’s not a condition that can be ignored or wished away. Carney is serious when he talks about a historic “rupture in the world order”, as he did at Davos early this year.

Canadians understand that maintaining our sovereignty and independence will entail consequences and sacrifices. We did not bring this trade war on ourselves; we have merely refused to comply in advance to the unreasonable demands of a bad-faith actor. We will be punished for it. We have accepted this. If nothing else, let the US’s retaliation be a warning to the rest of the western alliance. Run, run. Protect yourselves. Move faster.

Jen Gerson is a Canadian commentator and co-founder of The Line. She lives in Calgary, Alberta

The other Post Office scandal: how organised crime launders money on the high street

The Guardian Tue, 25 Aug 2026 04:00:49 GMT

Hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being deposited at post offices every year. So why are the police reluctant to investigate the scale of the problem?

Last chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off. Click here to order

Leicestershire police won’t say who first told them about Jigar Gheewala, but you can see why, once they had heard of him, they decided to find out more. Gheewala was unemployed, had no apparent income, yet lived in a £1.3m house and sent his three children to private school. “He was a declared bankrupt, with a bank account that was absolutely not reflective of what it should be,” said financial crime supervisor Laura Panter of Leicestershire police’s economic crime team. “That was our starting point.”

Over the course of 2020, despite being on benefits, Gheewala’s bank account received more than £880,000 in cash in 200 different deposits. He was, it turned out, a money launderer, but not the kind you’ll see in the movies. Gheewala’s deposits had been made not in Liechtenstein or on Grand Cayman, but at various post office branches in Leicester, one thick wodge of banknotes after another.

As banks have closed branches all over Britain, post offices have quietly become central to how we move our money. In 2017, post offices began to accept deposits on behalf of banks, and those deposits now exceed £30bn a year. The way it works is straightforward. A customer hands over banknotes to be counted, then inserts a bank card and enters the pin, like a cashpoint in reverse. The post office system then communicates with the bank’s system, which credits the value of the cash to the account linked to the card.

It is a simple system, which Post Office Ltd, the state-owned company that controls the branches, says provides a crucial service to businesses and individuals otherwise cut off from banking services. But the simplicity comes at a cost. It has eliminated many of the checks that previously stopped criminals from laundering their cash. In the same way you can use someone else’s card to take money from a cashpoint, provided you know the pin, you can use any bank card to make a deposit at the post office. The process is deliberately streamlined and, unlike at a bank, the post office operative (often referred to as postmaster or subpostmaster) has no way to access any of the account details, and thus no way to check if the person with the card is its holder, or whether this transaction is part of a suspicious pattern.

Law enforcement agencies estimate that, alongside ordinary businesses’ takings, hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being paid into the post office each year. This allows drug dealers and other criminals to bank their illicit wealth, and profit from their crimes, and to do so with the absolute minimum of effort. “The number of places where cash can come into the economy is vast now but, as bank branches continue to close, the number of places to pay it back in has necessarily become more restricted. You’ve got this sort of reverse funnel effect going on,” said a former Post Office employee with knowledge of how it organises financial services. “The bad guys are genuinely targeting post offices as one of the few places left where they can actually go to put money in.”

Leicestershire police used Gheewala’s transactions to reconstruct how he operated. On a typical day, he might make his first cash deposit in the east of the city, at a post-office counter hosted by a convenience store; then it would be a five-minute drive to another store, with boxes of veg out the front, its windows obscured by decals of soft drinks and spirits, offering post office services alongside the scratchcards. A few minutes away was another branch, between a chemist and a fried chicken shop, before another short drive would bring him to a retail centre where the post office sat next to a bakery on a prosperous-looking residential street. A final drive north would take him to a convenience store among red-brick detached houses, and that was a morning’s work done: thousands of pounds deposited in an hour or so, bundles of criminal cash being paid into the most ordinary of locations.

“When we started looking at this, we were then able to see other individuals in Leicestershire that were mimicking exactly the same activity,” said Panter. “What we were finding was there was quite a consistent pattern in terms of the deposit activity around post offices.”

Panter and her colleagues’ investigation became Operation Kilo, which began in 2021 and culminated in December 2025 with Gheewala being sentenced to almost 12 years in prison, along with six co-conspirators. And this was not just a Leicester-based operation. Officers watched as couriers came to Leicester with bags full of cash earned by criminals from London and Yorkshire, stashing them in shops for Gheewala’s people to pick up. Each day’s haul would be distributed among a network of underlings, who trekked around the city’s post offices, paying rubber-band-bound stacks of banknotes into as many as 10 different accounts at each stop, using cards with the pins written on the back.

The bank accounts into which the money was deposited belonged to ordinary people – “mules” in police jargon – who received small payments for renting them out, or to companies in Leicester’s garment business, where managers faked invoices to make the payments look legitimate. (Gheewala promised the mules £50 per £10,000 laundered, but in reality he often seems to have paid them less than that.) Gheewala controlled the whole operation from a laptop kept in an otherwise empty house, with all the account details and their passwords written down in a notebook. As soon as the money appeared online he would, using cryptocurrency exchanges, disperse it around the world.

In two years, Gheewala’s group moved an astonishing £53m, allowing organised criminals to legitimise their earnings on an industrial scale. It’s not clear how much exactly Gheewala was charging for the service, although to judge by the lifestyle he was living, he was doing well out of it.

His operation might have been big, but it wasn’t unique. Just a month after Gheewala’s conviction, two men were jailed in Birmingham for an almost-identical scheme, in which they paid in up to £200,000 a day as they travelled between 10 post offices in the east of the city. In April, a man from Cheltenham was jailed for six years and eight months for controlling a network of mules paying millions of pounds of cash into post offices in Bristol and Gloucestershire.

And this has been going on for a while. Two men were jailed at Southwark crown court in 2024 for paying £26m into post offices in London and Manchester before their arrests in 2017. Students have been jailed in Scotland for paying criminal money into post offices, and there are other ongoing cases in which similar crimes are alleged.

If it wasn’t for what has been going on elsewhere in the Post Office, this would be a major story. Instead, it has been largely ignored.

The Post Office Horizon scandal burst into the public consciousness thanks to 2024’s ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office, but by that stage it had been dragging on for two decades. Post Office Ltd wrongly prosecuted hundreds of its post office operatives, despite senior figures knowing that the computer program that supposedly showed they had been committing fraud was faulty. Ex-post office operative Alan Bates’s landmark victory against his former employers in 2019 forced the government to overturn his and others’ convictions, and to promise to pay hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation.

The scandal is one of Britain’s worst miscarriages of justice. One of its unfortunate side effects is that it has impeded investigations into how much money is being laundered via post office branches. Even if police officers are themselves confident that figures originating in Post Office Ltd’s Horizon software (a version of which is still being used) are reliable, they are aware that many jury members will – for understandable reasons – be intensely sceptical. Documents released by the inquiry into the Horizon scandal show that, in 2024, just a few weeks after the ITV drama was first aired, a detective constable from Blackburn police station decided to halt an investigation into “large-scale money laundering, and possibly other fraud offences” via post office branches in Lancashire out of concern that defence lawyers would find it too easy to discredit evidence originating from the computer system.

“After the Mr Bates TV show, it became a real hot potato and nobody wanted to get hold of it,” said one officer, who asked to remain anonymous. “For every case that’s brought, there are many more in the background. There is no real appetite to do anything unless it’s a slam dunk, because the public is on the side of the post office operatives.” So the problem remains. “It’s the way that you can pay money into the post office without checks, that’s the problem. It’s huge.”

If you look at the raw numbers, you can see his point. In October 2020, cash deposits at post-office branches across the UK totalled £1.9bn. That is £1.9bn for that single month, not the whole year. The following October, the sum was £2.2bn. That number kept rising each year until, by October 2025, it came to £2.9bn – an increase of 50% in just five years. Although Post Office Ltd then stopped publishing such detailed figures, the trend has continued. It boasted of a 10% increase in deposits in the first quarter of this year, meaning they have now almost certainly passed £3bn a month.

What makes these numbers so astounding is that over the same period, cash usage among the general public has dropped sharply. Cash now accounts for fewer than one in 10 transactions in the UK. Yet cash deposits at the post office have gone sharply in the opposite direction.

According to Post Office Ltd, the reason it stopped publishing monthly cash totals last year was because its post office operatives did not want to alert criminals to the amount of money they had on the premises. Branches are vulnerable to theft for the same reason they are wide open to money laundering. They are often just ordinary shops offering post-office services over the counter, and they lack the specialised equipment that would allow them to track who is on the premises, or to keep their employees safe.

Back when Post Office Ltd was still publishing its monthly cash figures, it would accompany them with upbeat quotes about how much it was helping small businesses by providing banking services. While much of the increase is certainly being driven by the closure of bank branches, a senior police officer would regularly forward the figures to me, accompanied with a single emoji: 👀.

Concerns about being seen to further victimise post office operatives has discouraged police officers from going on the record about the scale of the problem that they’re seeing. “I’m sure you appreciate that anything quotable is going to have to be suitably vanilla,” another senior officer told me. “It would need to be, you know, ‘we work in partnership’, ‘there are many perspectives’-type stuff.”

The sensitivity is understandable, but it comes with dangers. By making it possible for organised criminals – drug dealers, human traffickers, thieves, fraudsters and others – to launder their earnings, and thus to keep their profits, the post office risks creating an entirely different scandal.

The trial of Giuseppe Sangiovanni and seven of his alleged co-conspirators was due to start in May 2025 at Bristol crown court, and to run for several days. Sangiovanni was accused of running a scheme that laundered £2.2m via post office branches in Bristol and Gloucestershire over a few months of 2021. His alleged co-conspirators were accused of letting him move money through their bank accounts in return for small payments.

On the first morning of the trial, however, Sangiovanni changed his plea to guilty and left the courtroom to await a fresh hearing, leaving his co-defendants behind. It quickly became clear that they were not criminal masterminds. I had only just arrived in Bristol and knew only the bare outlines of the case, but even I could tell their chances of escaping conviction were now close to nonexistent. If the prosecutors had all the transaction details, and the ringleader was admitting the charges, then the owners of the bank accounts through which the money had passed would find it all but impossible to convince a jury that nothing untoward had occurred.

Technically, a trial was still scheduled, but it was so obviously not going to happen that the jury never even entered the courtroom. The two prosecution lawyers, far from wargaming the new reality, were using the break to discuss holiday destinations for their unexpected spell of spare time. The only people present who appeared not to realise the consequences of Sangiovanni’s decision were his co-defendants, who continued to sit in the dock like baby birds in smart casual, with only the haziest of ideas what was going on.

The judge tried to help, encouraging them to discuss things with their lawyers. They whispered among themselves, until one at a time – over the course of many hours, and after many hearings were convened, suspended and convened again – they changed their pleas to guilty too. (They were not masterminds, as I say, and mostly received suspended sentences.)

“They’re just run-of-the-mill local criminals. A couple of them weren’t really criminals at all. One that we didn’t charge was a single mum and, to a degree, was exploited,” said Detective Inspector Peter Highway of the south west regional organised crime unit. It was only while being interviewed by police that one defendant discovered that Sangiovanni had laundered more than £1m through his bank account. “He was a bit surprised by that number,” said Highway, “because he hadn’t done the deposits himself.”

Money laundering was criminalised in the UK in 1988 as part of a global effort to close loopholes in the financial system that were allowing criminals to keep their profits. Previously, it had been easy for criminals to walk into a bank and pay in cash, no questions asked, but the new laws obliged bankers to report suspicious transactions to law enforcement agencies. The theory was that, with bankers sending in a steady stream of suspicious activity reports, police officers would be able to see money being laundered in real time, freeze it and arrest its owners.

The world has moved on since then and the most sophisticated crime, such as fraud, involves electronic money stolen from people’s bank accounts and moved in a bewildering variety of ways, involving shell companies, cryptocurrencies, secrecy jurisdictions and more. This requires equally advanced countermeasures from banks, which use AI-powered tools to spot the signs of criminal behaviour.

At the street level, however, not much has changed: criminals still use cash, and the National Crime Agency estimates that they launder about £12bn worth of banknotes in the UK each year, largely by presenting the money as the fruits of legitimate businesses. This is where branches of the post office come in.

From the criminals’ point of view, post offices are quick and easy places to launder dodgy money. “There’s no requirement for ID verification, there’s no requirement for any kind of enhanced screening, there’s no centralised CCTV,” said the second senior police officer. We put a higher bar on buying alcohol than we do on money laundering via the post office.

This is why Gheewala’s mules were able to go into a branch with a pocket full of bank cards, and pay bundles of cash into multiple accounts, one after another. “You definitely don’t want, in a post office that has already got queues out the door, to have a complicated financial transaction going on. So everything that the post office does for banking is done with simplicity in mind,” said the former Post Office employee.

The trouble then is, as happened in Leicester, that criminals move money onwards as soon as it arrives in a bank account. Any reports that post office employees do make about the transaction will come too late for the bank to be able to freeze it. This defangs the UK’s entire anti-money-laundering strategy, which has always relied on being able to block suspicious transactions while officers investigate them.

The criminal possibilities opened up by Post Office Ltd’s foray into banking were quickly obvious. In July 2020, the Post Office’s compliance committee noted £7m of questionable deposits had gone into 45 branches. In November that year, it discussed how £5-7m a week was being deposited at just two branches in east London, and said it was discussing with the banks what action to take.

Sangiovanni and his co-defendants fell foul of this kind of scrutiny, after bank compliance officers spotted what amounted to millions of pounds of suspicious cash transactions at 27 post offices around Gloucestershire, and alerted the police who brought in first the mules, then Sangiovanni, for questioning. “He gave an account that he would go to a car park at Asda, and someone would give him a carrier bag full of cash, and he would then take it away, and then send them some crypto,” said Highway. “He didn’t feel that was suspicious. We did.”

By the time officers from the south west organised crime unit moved in, however, the money was long gone. So, although they caught Sangiovanni, the criminals whose cash he was laundering got to enjoy the freshly laundered money. “Millions of pounds into the laundering, that’s a bit late in the day,” said Highway.

It looks obvious how to close this gap in our defences against dirty cash. If the Post Office is going to act like a bank, it should collect the same kind of information as a bank, make the same kind of reports as a bank, and freeze transactions in the same way that banks do. In 2023, the regulators at the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) took a small step in this direction, by imposing limits on how much cash could be deposited at the post office at any one time. It was a logical step to take, but it ran into immediate controversy.

The fact that two-thirds of bank branches have closed in the UK in the past decade has left businesses and individuals who still rely on cash heavily dependent on post-office branches to pay in their takings. Post Office Ltd used this fact to push back against the FCA’s deposit limits by saying they were penalising hard-pressed businesses that were just trying to stay afloat. “They are hurting legitimate customers and businesses who need support,” said Ross Borkett, Post Office Ltd’s then-head of banking, after the FCA’s changes were announced. Cash-intensive businesses, via the British Independent Retailers Association and the Independent Retail Consortium, mobilised a lobbying operation, writing to their MPs, who in turn held debates in parliament to highlight how few bank branches were left in their constituencies.

As a result, ministers promised to ensure that businesses and individuals still reliant on banknotes and coins would always be able to use them. In other words, the FCA’s cash limit is likely to be the last intervention to make payments at post offices harder.

At a time when an increasingly large proportion of the population can’t access a physical bank branch, the 11,500 post-office branches in the UK will become ever-more central to a strategy of ensuring everyone can still use banknotes. Moving, securing and accepting cash is expensive though, which is one reason why the banks don’t much want to do it any more. Post offices don’t charge their customers for making deposits, however, so who is going to pay for it?

The answer to that question is tied up in the legacy of the Horizon scandal. Post Office Ltd was already in significant financial difficulties before it began having to pay compensation to the hundreds of post office operatives that it had unfairly prosecuted. It has now had to distribute more than £1bn, pushing it into a deep annual loss.

That is already a significant challenge for its long-term viability, but it is only half of the problem it faces. Post-office branches operate as independent businesses, but the amount of money operatives earned from providing post office services fell by almost 5% in the decade to 2023, in part thanks to fewer people sending letters. Meanwhile, post office operatives’ expenses have increased. So Post Office Ltd not only needs to find the money to pay compensation to the post office operatives it has wronged, but it must also simultaneously find a sustainable business model if it wants people to be post office operatives at all. And that is where banking comes in.

Banks pay Post Office Ltd for providing services on their behalf, which helped it to post revenues of £309m from “banking and ATMs” in its 2024-5 accounts. That was more than a third of its revenues for that year, and only slightly less than it earned from handling the mail. In fact, Post Office Ltd may already be making more money from deposits and withdrawals than it does from its traditional business. As the former insider joked: “We should start calling it the Bank Office.”

This isn’t just important for Post Office Ltd, but also for individual post office operatives, who earn a fee for every cash deposit they accept. “The post office operatives will be remunerated on the transactions that they have through their branch, so they will get a transaction fee,” Ben Woollard, the new head of banking at Post Office Ltd, told me. “As with any product, the more a post office operative or any business will deliver, then they will earn more income out of that.”

Woollard argues that post-office branches are no different from any other business in being vulnerable to money laundering. He pointed out to me that anyone offering banking services receives annual training in how to recognise and tackle money laundering, and that the head office sends out alerts to branches in areas that appear to have a large number of suspicious transactions.

But although any business that handles cash could be exploited by criminals, it is also true that few businesses handle banknotes in the volumes that routinely pass through post-office branches, making them more vulnerable to abuse than most. Post office operatives are also running a system that we know is already wide open to dirty money, and are rewarded proportionally to the raw total of money they put through it, so the temptation to look the other way or even to provide financial services to criminals must be ever-present.

We have no idea how many insiders have given in to this temptation, and it looks likely that we will remain in the dark. The disastrous legacy of the Horizon scandal means there has been little appetite to investigate. With such a deeply flawed system, the best that police officers can hope for is to prosecute the more egregious offenders.

So despite the success of Operation Kilo, Leicestershire police’s Detective Constable Catherine Richards wasn’t exactly optimistic that Gheewala’s conviction would change anything: “Crime is continuing,” she told me. “Money needs to be laundered. And, yeah, somebody else fills those boots, don’t they?”

At Home and Abroad, Deference to Trump Turns Increasingly to Defiance

The New York Times August 25, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

While the president remains the most dominant figure in the world, other leaders and institutions are pushing back more vigorously than at the beginning of his second term.

By Peter Baker

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent and is covering his sixth presidency.

This is a summer movie that’s been seen before: President Trump makes demands. When the other side does not give him what he wants, he escalates with bombastic threats of crippling punishment. The other side surrenders.

Except that Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada, evidently has not read the script. His refusal to buckle in the face of Mr. Trump’s trade ultimatum even at the cost of retaliatory tariffs has flipped the narrative of the president’s second term. Instead of giving in, Mr. Carney is testing whether defiance is a viable strategy against Mr. Trump.

The age of capitulation that defined Mr. Trump’s return to office may be starting to fade. World leaders and domestic institutions are, in some cases at least, showing less willingness to submit to Mr. Trump’s will. European leaders have refused to join his war with Iran. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel flatly rejected his Gaza plan. Gulf Arab states forced him to abandon plans to charge a shipping toll in the Strait of Hormuz.

Universities and law firms are rebuffing his directives rather than signing on the bottom line. Bond markets are rebelling against his fiscal policies. Even the ABC network, whose $16 million payment to settle a Trump lawsuit was seen as an early example of yielding to the president, has discovered that it did not buy peace and is now suing his administration for threatening its broadcast licenses.

None of which means that Mr. Trump should be underestimated. Although his poll numbers are at or near historic lows, he remains the most dominant figure on the planet, able to reset the terms of the global conversation on a whim with a social media post and unafraid of wielding power in ways that his predecessors did not.

He may yet bring Canada and Israel to heel through force of personality, tariffs or other means. The Supreme Court has given him one free pass after another to use his executive authority as he sees fit, whether it be taking control of independent agencies, building his cherished ballroom or trying to crack down on mail-in voting.

And every time someone predicts that Republicans in Congress will finally begin exhibiting some independence, they prove the prognosticators wrong. While they have resisted his pressure in some instances lately, Senate confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general made clear that he still dominates his party’s congressional wing.

But even among Republicans, there are some worrisome signs for the president. Although he has successfully punished several prominent Republican lawmakers he deemed disloyal by rallying his MAGA base to defeat them in party primaries this year, G. O. P. voters have rejected Mr. Trump’s endorsed candidates in 10 nominating contests, including six in August alone. Polls show his support among Republicans slipping.

“I think that recent weeks have been somewhat of an inflection point,” said Norm Eisen, a former Obama White House lawyer and founder of a group called the Democracy Defenders Fund, who has been waging multiple court fights against Mr. Trump. “At home and abroad, pro-democracy forces and everybody else are standing up to him with much more widespread vigor.”

Among others, Mr. Eisen has been involved in legal battles over the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, birthright citizenship, the Federal Reserve and the aborted prosecution of a former Olympian charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. To the extent that there has been a shift, Mr. Eisen said, it owes in part to overreaching by Mr. Trump. “Trump has been his own worst enemy,” he said.

Mr. Trump and his advisers reject that assessment, of course, and point to his continuing ability to shape events. In a series of social media posts in recent days, the president has taken credit for falling crime rates and insisted that he is winning the war with Iran. He has disputed polls showing his unpopularity and rejected stories about recent primary losses.

“The actual Polls are tremendous, and the Spirit in our Country has never been higher,” he wrote. “We’re winning against EVERYONE, including Iran, whose Country is in Economic and Military Death Spiral.”

He said that his “endorsements are stronger than ever” and asserted that the Republican candidates who were defeated despite his support were never going to prevail. “The few that lost were done out of loyalty,” he wrote. “It was almost impossible for them to win but, I felt obligated to go with them because they were, in my opinion, good people!”

Mr. Trump did not have to explain away losses when he first returned to the White House last year. In his early months, it seemed that he was winning across the board. Even without a strong mandate — he won a second term with just 49.9 percent of the popular vote — he managed to impose his will across society.

He dictated to private businesses how they should make decisions and universities how they should teach. He made diversity programs so radioactive that employers around the country dropped them. He gutted federal agencies without asking Congress, took over the Kennedy Center and used the power of government to go after his enemies. And in the process, he succeeded in pressuring others to follow his desires. Law firms, universities, media firms and tech billionaires bent over backward to show deference as they changed policies to suit him or agreed to multimillion-dollar deals that he demanded.

Jacob Weisberg, who chronicled the trend of submission in a new book coming out next month called “Profiles in Cowardice,” said that the incentives have begun to reverse and that giving into Mr. Trump can now generate a costly backlash. “The price has risen on the other side for capitulation,” he said, citing as an example the wave of criticism when Yale University began negotiating with the Trump administration.

Still, he cautioned against overstating how much has changed yet. “There’s some signs, but there have been signs before and people have gotten ahead of themselves,” Mr. Weisberg said. “I believe it will start to turn around at some point, and I think it’s tied to Trump’s popularity. I’ve always thought that when he gets down below 30s, you’ll start to see different behavior. And there are some indications that’s happening.”

There are indications that is happening overseas as well, at least in Europe and, to a lesser extent, the Middle East. When Mr. Trump became president again last year, NATO allies bowed to his pressure and agreed to increase military spending. But now they are more resistant to his demands across the board, from Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain on the left to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy on the right.

“It’s good politics for a lot of these European leaders to stand up to him,” said Matthew Kroenig, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security and a former national security official under three presidents of both parties, including Mr. Trump. “We see that most clearly in Spain, but also in other places in Europe.”

That seemed to change early in the year when Mr. Trump pushed to take over Greenland, which is part of Denmark, a NATO ally. Mr. Trump even held out the possibility of using military power to seize the expansive island, raising the prospect of NATO at war with itself. Rather than trying to placate him, as they had in the past, European leaders spoke out forcefully against Mr. Trump and some even sent a small number of troops to Greenland for military exercises to make the point.

“Greenland was a turning point, in part because it was an attack on the sovereignty of Europe itself and Europeans began to understand at that point there was simply no end to Trump’s rapaciousness and to his demands,” said Jeremy Shapiro, a former State Department official now at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

Mr. Kroenig said he has heard the same from European leaders. “That’s one they come back to over and over again,” he said. “It’s one thing to say we need to spend more on defense, it’s one thing to have a trade war. But a NATO ally threatening military force against another NATO ally, that’s crossing a line.”

For all that, he noted, European leaders are not looking for a fight with Mr. Trump either, and they have stuck with their commitment to increase military spending. “It does seem like they’re going all in,” Mr. Kroenig said. And he noted that Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany, while criticizing the Iran war, is allowing American forces to use bases in the country.

The clash with Canada brings a lot of that history to the fore. Both sides have continued to escalate in recent days. In a speech announcing that he had broken off talks last week, Mr. Carney said he had long warned that “America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that that will never ever happen.”

Mr. Trump on Tuesday denounced Mr. Carney as a “weak and ineffective prime minister” and threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America since “we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said that Mr. Trump had offered Canada an attractive deal. “With so much of Canada’s economy reliant on exporting to the United States — which has an over 12-times larger economy and seven-times larger population — Canada’s position is less about defiance and more about short-term foolishness,” he said in an email.

Leaders across the world are watching. Mr. Shapiro said they “mostly now believe that backing down in the face of Trumpian aggression or insults only encourages more demands.” He added: “I think Carney is setting the template for how they will respond to future Trumpian tariff threats.”

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

‘Darth Vader’ Wants You to Know He Definitely Supports Flock Surveillance

Wired August 25, 2026

At the San Diego City Council’s most recent budget meeting, Sith Lord Darth Vader had some points to make. Between gasping breaths, Vader praised the council’s recent votes to renew its contract with the surveillance company Flock Safety, which has been making headlines recently as more and more stories of police officers abusing its tools have continued to come out—and as a WIRED review of code for a new AI tool already in use by some police departments has made clear that it is watching far more than just license plates.

“The emperor is a fan of Flock. And we must continue utilizing Flock technologies so that we can follow and surveil the rebel scum as they move from playground to playground, from playground to pool, from pool to gymnasium.”

The recording of the video has gone viral, reaching millions of people on TikTok and Instagram.

The man behind the stunt is Anthony Ralphs, a San Diego-based DJ, event producer, and agriculture consultant who has spent the better part of the past year advocating against the city’s support of Flock’s use by the San Diego Police Department.

Initially, Ralphs thought about keeping his identity hidden behind the Vader mask—a 2004 Hasbro model. But he says that as the video has picked up more and more steam, he decided to “take ownership” of the stunt that put Flock and surveillance technology on the minds and feeds of millions of people around the world.

WIRED spoke to Ralphs about advocacy, crafting a costume, and the role that art can play in civic engagement.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

VITTORIA ELLIOTT: How did this start for you? Was this your first city council meeting?

ANTHONY RALPHS: No. My first time attending a city council meeting was sometime last summer or last fall. But really the most consequential city council meeting that I attended, that really got me in the fold of starting to regularly participate in my civic duties, was this issue of Flock. It was my third, or maybe my fourth, city council meeting back on December 9th, and the city council was putting this up to a vote, whether to continue to use Flock.

The story back then was that the city council didn't exactly know what the technology was. The police were touting it as a force multiplier. There were over 300 people at that vote, the meeting room was completely full, and I would say 95 percent of the people there were saying they didn’t want Flock. But the council voted for it anyway. It was extremely discouraging, and it really lit a fire under me to start going and regularly participating.

I came to the following city council meeting, and I was one of maybe five people in the city council chambers, and there had been close to 300 just a couple of weeks prior. That moment was eye-opening. I realized not everyone can be there all the time to do this, and that's what we need. We need consistent advocacy. So I took time off of school to be able to do that.

Why did this feel so critical?

Our city's $120 million deficit. They cut several arts programs, and while they did that, they also provided the $2.2 million for Flock's contract, even when people in those communities that are being most heavily policed say that they don’t want this. And now, we have the case of Hugo Parra, a local San Diegan who was falsely imprisoned and sat in prison for 30 days due to an erroneous tag by the Flock cameras. [Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this matter.]

He and his friend, who was also arrested, are both suing this city for $1.5 million. So by the time the city ends up settling those two lawsuits, it will probably add another million dollars to that contract.

What were you studying?

I was taking classes at San Diego Mesa College and San Diego City College, I had been studying theater and labor studies, and I got my certificate in labor studies. As a student, I interned for the American Federation of Teachers, the local chapter here in San Diego. Our job was to organize and we would get real hands-on training going to strike lines and showing solidarity. We would canvas for candidates, and we were doing phone banks, so we got a really comprehensive experience of what it's like to participate civically in the real world. I would DJ for the people on the picket line once a week before school, and that really showed me the power of art specifically to make a political impact.

What ultimately led to the choice to attend the council meeting as Darth Vader?

I was always interested in guerrilla theater, I studied it in a playwriting class in school. But this was really a last resort. I had been going to meetings for months, and I have a lot of sympathy for these representatives, because I am the vice chair of my local planning group. I know what it’s like to sit there and get dunked on by random people. So, I did my homework on all of them. I learned what they voted for, what they've voted against, the progressive policies that they had enacted that I could support. I went so far as to bring them flowers.

But at a certain point, it felt like we've exhausted all of the efforts. We did it the right way, and they still continued to ignore their constituents.

I was in the shower one day and it hit me. I was trying to think of how I could satirize their points, because I realized they seemed to have a lack of self-awareness. I realized we're not getting through to them, and they are not listening to us and there's no consequences for them not listening to us. So, maybe we need to show them how silly they're being.

How did you prepare?

I am a huge Star Wars fan. I used to watch the movies almost every day as a kid. In the lead-up to the meeting, I rewatched all the movies again, the original ones, trying to get his gesticulations down. I got a silk cape, I think it was from Turkey. I found the original 2004 Hasbro helmet, and I chose this one because it had a voice changer in it. But I had been told the voice changer was a little bit gimmicky, so I thought “I'll just replicate his voice myself.” I wasn’t able to get everything I wanted for the costume, but I knew that the August 19th meeting was going to be the big one, because the ACLU was going to be at that committee meeting. So I pulled together some stuff I already had, and I think it turned out well.

The helmet actually came in handy, because there were buttons on it to make noises. At certain points, I'd stand up to go to the bathroom and I'd hit the breathing button—you know, the Darth Vader breathing sound. At one point I turned around, and I'm right within earshot of the chief of police, and I pushed the button and it said, “Your powers are weak!”

What do you hope this achieves?

I want to make it cool to engage in one's civic responsibility again. City council meetings don't have to be stale rooms with boring thoughts presented in unoriginal ways. They can be places where we bring our own art, where we bring the strength of our intellect and our moral fortitude with our talent and creativity.

This sparked a global conversation about luxury surveillance and living under Big Brother, and in Orwellian-digital, fully surveilled hellscape. Some people didn't know what Flock was a week ago. We've reframed the narrative from “this is a ‘necessary evil’” to “If Darth Vader finds it a ‘necessary evil,’ that should make us pause and reflect on whether or not we need it.”
